# Asymptotic Rank of Complete Graph Tensors

Huanyi Zhou<sup>∗</sup>

**Abstract**

Graph tensors extend the matrix multiplication tensor by placing a two-party identity tensor on every edge of a graph and keeping one tensor leg at every vertex. We study the asymptotic rank of the tensor associated with the complete graph. For every integer \(n\ge 2\), over the complex numbers, we prove

The upper bound matches the maximum-cut lower bound for every even _n_ and differs from it by only 1/4 for every odd _n_. In particular, the exponent per edge is below 2/3 for every \(n\ge 5\), answering a question of Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam.

Our proof extends the polynomial multiplication approach underlying OpenAI’s bound \(\omega\le 9/4\). The main step separates any fixed number of shared tensor legs simultaneously, using only linearly many direct-sum copies in the number of blocks. This yields an entropy inequality for higher-order tensors. We apply it to the tensor for multiplying _n_-1 polynomials, whose rank is linear in the input length. Discrete concavity and a shifted tripling inequality then force a lower bound on a symmetrized spectral profile. Comparing this growth with polynomial interpolation gives the stated upper bound while preserving all _n_ tensor legs.

We also prove an operational barrier for these higher-order polynomial constructions. For \(n\ge 3\), the specified formal reduction rules cannot certify an exponent below _n_<sup>2</sup>/4 for GT<sub>2</sub>(_K<sub>n</sub>_), even after taking tensor powers and allowing subexponential overhead and common auxiliary factors. This extends the symmetric three-leg barrier of Amanov, van den Berg, and Zuiddam and explains the remaining gap for odd complete graphs within this method.

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Graph tensors and previous bounds

The rank of a tensor is the minimum number of simple tensors whose entrywise sum represents it in fixed coordinates. A simple tensor is a product of first-order tensors, with one factor for each leg. For a bilinear map, tensor rank measures the number of products of linear forms needed to compute its outputs. This connection has played a central role in the study of matrix multiplication since Strassen’s algorithm \[Str69, BCS97\]. When several copies of a tensor are computed together, their rank can be smaller than the product of their individual ranks. The corresponding asymptotic rank is

\(\widetilde{\mathrm{R}}(T)=\mathrm{lim}_{N\rightarrow\infty}\mathrm{R}(T^{\otimes_KN})^{1/N}.\)

Here a _leg_ is one coordinate direction of the tensor, and the Kronecker product \(\otimes_K\) pairs corresponding indices while preserving the number of legs. Definitions 2.2, 2.12, and 2.13 give the precise conventions. Throughout this paper, ranks are taken over the complex numbers.

Graph tensors provide a natural family in which to study this behavior beyond bilinear maps \[CVZ19, CZ19\]. Let _q_ be a positive integer. For a simple undirected graph _G_, place the two- party tensor \(\sum_{i=0}^{q-1}e_i^{(q)}\otimes_Ce_i^{(q)}\) on every edge, and group all indices incident with the same vertex into one leg. The resulting tensor GT_<sub>q</sub>(G_) has one leg for each vertex. The basis vectors \(e_i^{(q)}\) and the construction operation \(\otimes_C\) are defined in Definition 2.3; the complete coordinate definition of GT_<sub>q</sub>(G_) appears in Definition 2.20. In quantum information, this tensor describes pairwise maximally entangled states shared along the edges of a network. Rank and subrank describe conversions between these pairwise resources and a state shared by all parties \[VC17, CVZ19\].

For a triangle, each leg is indexed by a pair. With \(e_{(i,j)}=e_{iq+j}^{(q^2)}\) for \(0\le i,j\le q-1\), local coordinate permutations give

\(\mathsf{GT}_q(K_3)\cong\sum_{0\le i,j,h\le q-1}e_{(i,j)}\otimes_Ce_{(j,h)}\otimes_Ce_{(h,i)}.\)

This is precisely the matrix multiplication tensor. Let \(\omega\) be the infimum of the real numbers \(\gamma\) such that, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), two \(q\times q\) complex matrices can be multiplied using \(O_\varepsilon(q^{\gamma+\varepsilon})\) arithmetic operations. Then \(\omega=\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\mathrm{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_3))\). Thus, determining the asymptotic rank of graph tensors extends the matrix multiplication problem to an arbitrary number of parties.

Strassen’s seven-product algorithm gave \(\omega\le\mathrm{log}_27<3\) \[Str69\]. Approximate bilinear algorithms and interpolation introduced the use of degenerations \[BCRL79, Bin80\]. Schönhage’s asymptotic sum inequality converted simultaneous independent products into upper bounds on \(\omega\) \[Sch81\]. Strassen’s laser method and the Coppersmith–Winograd construction then provided a framework based on extracting useful components from large tensor powers \[Str86, Str87, CW90\]. Subsequent work improved the tensor-power analysis, the extraction of components, and the treatment of asymmetric parameters \[Sto10, DS13, VW12, LG14, AW21, DWZ23, VXXZ24, ADW<sup>+</sup>25\].  1 records selected milestones.

<tbc>OpenAI \[Ope26a\] recently proved \(\omega\le 9/4\) through a different use of polynomial multiplication and Strassen’s asymptotic spectrum \[Str88\]. A finite construction first separates tensor blocks that are independent on two legs but share the third. The resulting entropy inequality is applied to polynomial multiplication tensors. A determinant construction gives discrete concavity in the input lengths, and a three-sector decomposition gives a shifted tripling inequality. Together, these inequalities force a spectral profile to grow faster than the interpolation rank bound permits unless \(\omega\le 9/4\). An earlier manuscript in the same release obtained a bound below 2.258 \[Ope26b\].

For graphs with more than three vertices, it is useful to compare the exponent per edge, \(\tau(G)=\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\text{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_2(G))/|E(G)|\), defined for graphs with at least one edge in Definition 2.22. Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam \[CVZ19, Corollary 1.2.6\] generalized the Coppersmith-Winograd method and proved \(\tau(K_n)\le\mathrm{log}_7(9/2)<0.772943\) for every integer \(n\ge 4\). Their proof combines higher-order auxiliary tensors with a lower bound on the asymptotic subrank of tight tensors. Brand et al. \[BCK<sup>+</sup>26, Appendix C of the full version\] subsequently refined the four-party analysis, yielding the uniform bound \(\tau(K_n)\le 0.772318\) for \(n\ge 4\). They also used graph tensors to study the distinction between asymptotic rank and arithmetic circuit complexity for tensors with more than three legs. Christandl and Zuiddam \[CZ19\] developed tensor surgery, which transfers rank bounds through operations on the underlying graphs.

Two cut parameters give a useful perspective on these upper bounds. For every graph _G_ with at least two vertices,

\(\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\text{R}}\big(\mathsf{GT}_2(G)\big)\ge\mathrm{MaxCut}(G),\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\text{Q}}\big(\mathsf{GT}_2(G)\big)=\mathrm{MinCut}(G).\)

Here \(\widetilde{\text{Q}}\) is the asymptotic subrank from Definition 2.13, and the cuts are defined in Definition 2.23. The rank lower bound follows by flattening across a cut. The subrank identity is due to Vrana and Christandl \[VC17\]; we give a graph version of their proof in Theorem B.4. Thus, the minimum cut completely determines the asymptotic subrank. Whether the maximum cut likewise determines the asymptotic rank is the question posed by Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam \[CVZ19, Question 1.3.2\]. For a triangle, this question is exactly whether \(\omega=2\).

A direct way to use a matrix multiplication bound for a larger complete graph is to cover its edges by triangles. The strength of this comparison depends on the matrix multiplication bound available at the time. Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam \[CVZ19, Corollary 1.2.6\] compared their higher-order Coppersmith–Winograd construction with the triangle-cover exponent 0.790955 obtained from Le Gall’s bound \[LG14\]; their bound 0.772943 was strictly better. The later improvement of Brand et al. \[BCK<sup>+</sup>26, Appendix C of the full version\] also uses higher-order Coppersmith–Winograd tensors and predates the OpenAI result. With \(\omega\le 9/4\) now available, the same covering argument \[CVZ19, Proposition 1.1.25\] gives the new baseline

\(\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\text{R}}\big(\mathsf{G}\mathsf{T}_2(K_n)\big)\le\frac{\omega}{3}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}\le\frac{3}{4}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}(n\ge 3).\)

Here the final inequality uses the OpenAI bound \[Ope26a\]; Theorem A.5 gives the full covering argument. This new baseline improves the preceding uniform bounds to 3/4 per edge, but still leaves a quadratic gap from \(\mathrm{MaxCut}(K_n)=\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor\). This leads to the question that motivates our work:

_Can the polynomial multiplication construction itself be extended to complete graph tensors, while keeping every vertex as a separate tensor leg?_

## 1.2 Our rank bound and its context

We answer this question affirmatively by extending the polynomial multiplication method of OpenAI \[Ope26a\] from third-order tensors to complex _n_-th order tensors. The auxiliary tensor now multiplies _n_-1 independently supplied polynomials. Extending the separation and growth arguments to these additional legs gives a stronger bound than triangle covering with the OpenAI exponent alone.

**Theorem 1.1** (complete graph tensors)**.** _For every integer_ \(n\ge 2\)_, over the complex numbers,_

\(\left\lfloor\frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor\le\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\text{R}}\big(\mathsf{G}\mathsf{T}_2(K_n)\big)\le\frac{n^2}{4}.\)

The theorem is proved as Theorem 4.11 in Subsection 4.5. The lower bound is the standard cut bound; our contribution is the upper bound. For every even _n_, the two bounds coincide. For every odd _n_, the gap between them is only 1/4. This remaining gap also motivates our second result: Theorem 1.2 shows that a specified system of these polynomial constructions and combination rules cannot improve the threshold _n_<sup>2</sup>/4.

2 compares the upper bounds on both the logarithmic asymptotic rank and the exponent per edge. Our bound gives \(\tau(K_n)\le n/(2(n-1))\). Compared with triangle covering, it decreases the logarithmic upper bound by _n(n_-3)/8 for every \(n\ge 3\). In particular, it is strictly better for every \(n\ge 4\), and the exponent per edge tends to 1/2 as _n_ grows. The maximum-cut lower bound has the same limit.

<tbc>Theorem 1.1 settles one explicit question from \[CVZ19\] and resolves a family of cases of another. First, Question 1.3.1 asks whether \(\tau(K_n)<2/3\) for some \(n\ge 5\). Our bound proves this for every \(n\ge 5\); the formal statement and proof appear in Corollary 4.13. Second, Question 1.3.2 asks whether the maximum-cut lower bound is always tight. We prove that it is tight for every even complete graph: for every positive integer _s_,

\(\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\text{R}}\big(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_{2s})\big)=s^2=\mathrm{MaxCut}(K_{2s}).\)

Corollary 4.12 records this consequence. The question for general graphs remains open, as does equality with the maximum cut for odd complete graphs.

**Relation to recent polynomial methods.** Several works have developed the polynomial approach after the OpenAI release. Uzna ́nski \[Uzn26\] derived rectangular matrix multiplication bounds, including exponent 2 for multiplying an \(N\times\lceil N^k\rceil\) matrix by a \(\lceil N^k\rceil\times N\) matrix whenever \(0\le k\le 1/2\). Lü \[Lü26\] improved the finite shared-leg separation construction and extended the argument to arbitrary characteristic. Pass \[Pas26\] gave a constructive elementary proof of \(\omega\le 9/4\) by polynomial packings and block recursion. Amanov, van den Berg, and Zuiddam \[ABZ26\] gave an exposition over every field, treated rectangular shapes, and proved an operational barrier for the degeneration ingredients and combination rules used in the three-leg argument. Separately, Zadeh \[Zad26\] reported a further optimization within the Coppersmith- Winograd framework; its exponent does not improve on 9/4. Solomonik and Bl ́ser \[SB26\] study explicit rank and border-rank constructions for several independent matrix products, together with their finite-precision behavior. Their focus is on finite-size aggregation, whereas our result bounds the asymptotic rank of a tensor with one separate leg for every graph vertex.

## 1.3 The polynomial method in higher order

The proof uses the additional input directions while keeping their tensor legs separate. Its central construction separates _n_-2 shared legs at once; the resulting inequalities then control a polynomial tensor with _n_-1 independent inputs. The spectral framework remains Strassen’s. Work of Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam \[CVZ23\] and Alman, Li, and Pratt \[ALP26\] places it<tbc>

in the broader study of higher-order tensor spectra, and Alman and Li \[AL26\] systematically use spectral inequalities to obtain asymptotic-rank speedups from direct-sum degenerations. We next describe the constructions and the growth estimate that give Theorem 1.1.

**Simultaneous separation of shared legs.** The first component is a higher-order version of the finite separation construction in \[Ope26a\]. Let \(n\ge 3\) and \(M\ge 1\) be integers. In fixed coordinates, form _A_ by placing tensors _A_<sub>0</sub>_,...,A_<sub>_M_-1</sub> in matched, pairwise disjoint sectors on its last two legs, while sharing their first _n_-2 legs. Theorem 3.1 constructs a degeneration

\(A^{\oplus_K((2n-1)M)}\unknown\oplus_Kh_{=0}^{M-1}(A_h\otimes_KE_{n-1,n}^{(M)}).\)

The edge tensor \(E_{n-1,n}^{(M)}\) is an _M_-dimensional identity tensor on the last two legs and a scalar on every other leg, as in Definition 2.20. The relation \(\unknown\) is a degeneration in the sense of Definition 2.15. On the right, the sectors are independent on all _n_ legs.

The construction assigns each shared leg a tentative sector label \(g_j\in\{0,\dots,M-1\}\) for \(1\le j\le n-2\). A Fourier projection retains precisely the terms satisfying

\(u-v+2\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}(g_j-h)=0,\)

where \(h,u,v\in\{0,\dots,M-1\}\). Local weights make the total degree of every surviving term equal to \(\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}(g_j-h)^2\). Degree zero therefore forces _g<sub>j</sub>=h_ for every shared leg and _u=v_. These are exactly the conditions needed for the direct sum and its additional identity tensor. Only linearly many source copies are used, although the tentative labels are assigned independently.

To describe the consequence, let \(\phi\in\Phi_n\) be a spectral point (Definition 2.18). For each pair \(1\le i<j\le n\), define the _spectral edge weight_ \(p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}=\mathrm{log}_2\phi(E_{i,j}^{(2)})\). This number measures the value that \(\phi\) assigns to a resource shared only by legs _i_ and _j_. Lemma 4.4 proves \(\phi(E_{i,j}^{(q)})=q^{p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}}\) for every positive integer _q_. If every block _A<sub>h</sub>_ is nonzero, applying separation to words of a fixed type gives

\(\phi(A)\ge\mathrm{exp}\big(p_{n-1,n}^{(\phi)}H(\theta)\big)\prod_{h=0}^{M-1}\phi(A_h)^{\theta_h}\)

for every probability vector \(\theta=(\theta_0,\dots,\theta_{M-1})\); see Corollary 3.2. Here \(H(\theta)=-\sum_{h=0}^{M-1}\theta_h\mathrm{ln}\theta_h\), with 0ln0=0.

**A low-rank tensor with many input directions.** Following the use of polynomial multiplication in OpenAI \[Ope26a, Section 4\], we retain a separate tensor leg for every input. For positive integers _a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-1</sub>, put \(D=1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(a_j-1)\). The polynomial multiplication tensor from Definition 4.1 is<tbc>

\(\mathcal{C}_n(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})=\sum_{0\le i_j<a_j1\le j\le n-1}e_{i_1}^{(a_1)}\otimes_C\cdots\otimes_Ce_{i_{n-1}}^{(a_{n-1})}\otimes_Ce_{i_1+\cdots+i_{n-1}}^{(D)}.\)

<tbc>Evaluation and interpolation show that its rank is exactly _D_. Thus, when every input length equals _a_, the rank is _O<sub>n</sub>(a_) despite the _n_-1 independent inputs. For a spectral point \(\phi\in\Phi_n\), define its average edge weight and its symmetric profile by<tbc>

\(t_\phi=\frac{1}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}}\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}p_{i,j}^{(\phi)},P_\phi(\mathbf{a})=\left(\prod_{\pi\in S_n}\phi\big(\pi\mathcal{C}_n(\mathbf{a})\big)\right)^{1/(n!t_\phi)},\)

where **a**=(_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-1</sub>), _S<sub>n</sub>_ is the set of permutations of the _n_ legs, and \(\pi\mathcal{C}_n\) denotes the tensor with its legs permuted by \(\pi\). Definition 4.5 gives the full construction. We prove that \(t_\phi>0\). The normalization yields \(P_\phi(1,\dots,1,b)=b\) for every positive integer _b_, while interpolation gives \(P_\phi(\mathbf{a})\le D^{1/t_\phi}\).

**Concavity and shifted tripling.** The two polynomial inequalities from \[Ope26a\] extend to this profile. First, \(P_\phi\) is discretely concave in each input length. We take the Kronecker product with a two-dimensional identity tensor on one input and the output, and consider the kernel and quotient of a diagonal substitution on homogeneous binary forms. Multiplication by each fixed tuple of the other inputs preserves this kernel. Consequently, a single choice of bases works for all tuples, and a local degeneration produces two blocks with neighboring input lengths. The entropy inequality turns these matched blocks into concavity.

Second, for positive integers _a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-2</sub>_,h_ and \(S=\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}(a_j-1)\), a three-sector decomposition gives

\(P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},3h+S)\ge 3P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},h).\)

The outer sectors are translated copies of the shorter polynomial tensor. The middle sector becomes the same tensor after reversing each shared input index and exchanging the last input with the output. The product over all leg permutations makes this exchange harmless. In both constructions, the first _n_-2 inputs remain separate legs.

**Growth along the diagonal.** We extend OpenAI’s growth argument \[Ope26a, Section 5\] to _n_-1 input lengths. Increase the coordinates of (_a,...,a_) one at a time until reaching (_a_+1_,...,a_+1). At each step, tripling and concavity imply a multiplicative increase of at least 1+2/(_na_). There are _n_-1 steps, and an elementary product estimate gives \(P_\phi(a,\dots,a)\ge a^{2(n-1)/n}\) for every positive integer _a_. Comparing this with \(P_\phi(a,\dots,a)\le((n-1)(a-1)+1)^{1/t_\phi}\) forces \(t_\phi\le n/(2(n-1))\). Since a complete graph tensor is the Kronecker product of its edge tensors,

\(\phi(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n))=2\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}\le 2^{n^2/4}.\)

Strassen’s spectral duality then gives the upper bound in Theorem 1.1.

## 1.4 A barrier for the polynomial constructions

The preceding argument gives the upper bound _n_<sup>2</sup>/4. For odd _n_, it leaves open whether a different combination of the same ingredients can reach the maximum cut. Amanov, van den Berg, and Zuiddam \[ABZ26, Theorem 5.4\] answer the corresponding three-leg question by defining a formal reduction system and a numerical certificate that is monotone under its rules. We extend their symmetric certificate to _n_ legs. Our system includes interpolation, concavity, shifted tripling, and a separation construction that retains an auxiliary polynomial tensor, together with specified rules for combining them. The next theorem shows that these rules cannot improve the threshold _n_<sup>2</sup>/4.

As in Theorem 1.1, we state the conclusion for edge dimension 2. The formal complete-graph expression **G**<sub>_n,_2</sub> and diagonal expression **I**_<sub>n</sub>(R_) from Definition 5.3 evaluate to GT<sub>2</sub>(_K<sub>n</sub>_) and the diagonal tensor of size _R_, respectively. The relation \(\unknown_{\mathrm{poly},n}\) from Definition 5.5 records derivations from the listed rules.

**Theorem 1.2** (barrier for the polynomial constructions)**.** _For every integer_ \(n\ge 3\) _and every positive integer R,_

\(\mathbf{G}_{n,2}\unknown_{\mathrm{poly},n}\mathbf{I}_n(R)\Longrightarrow\mathrm{log}_2R\ge\frac{n^2}{4}.\)

Theorem 5.11 in Subsection 5.4 proves this statement and its asymptotic version with subexponential overhead and common auxiliary factors. We next describe the certificate and explain how it accounts for each ingredient of the polynomial method. **Formal expressions and their numerical values.** An expression records how its tensor is constructed, including the coordinates shared in a partial direct sum. Its atoms are reflected polynomial tensors: the expression C_n(a_1_,...,a__n_-1) evaluates to C_n(a_1_,...,a__n_-1) after reversing the output coordinate. Definitions 5.1 and 5.2 specify these atoms and the set F_n_ of expressions. Besides full sums and Kronecker products, an expression may use \(X\boxdash_eY\) , which shares the coordinates outside the two legs in _e_ and uses disjoint matched sectors on those two legs. Its coordinate meaning is given in Definition 2.9. Distinct expressions remain distinct even when they evaluate to isomorphic tensors. Lemma 5.6 verifies that every permitted derivation gives a valid tensor degeneration. For the rest of this overview, fix \(n\ge 3\), and put _d=n_-1 and \(\eta_n=n/(2(n-1))\). The certificate V_n_ from Definition 5.9 assigns a positive real number to each expression. Full sums and products receive ordinary sums and products of values, whereas a partial sum receives a different power sum: \(\mathcal{V}_n(X\oplus_KY)=\mathcal{V}_n(X)+\mathcal{V}_n(Y),\)
\(\mathcal{V}_n(X\otimes_KY)=\mathcal{V}_n(X)\mathcal{V}_n(Y),\)
\(\mathcal{V}_n(X\boxdash_eY)=\left(\mathcal{V}_n(X)^{1/\eta_n}+\mathcal{V}_n(Y)^{1/\eta_n}\right)^{\eta_n}.\) These formulas apply whenever the expressions are defined. The choice of \(\eta_n\) will make the cost of separating shared coordinates agree with the value of the edge retained by separation. The remaining task is to assign values to the polynomial atoms so that every permitted rule preserves the required inequality. **A comparison function for all input lengths.** For \(\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\dots,a_d)\in[1,\infty)^d\), sort the entries as \(b_1\le\cdots\le b_d\). Definition 5.7 introduces \(L_j=(d+2-j)b_j+\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}b_i-(d-1),c_j=\frac{2}{(d+1-j)(d+2-j)}(1\le j\le d),\)
\(H_d(\mathbf{a})=\prod_{j=1}^d\left(\frac{L_j}{2}\right)^{c_j}.\) For positive integer input lengths, set \(\mathcal{V}_n(\mathsf{C}_n(\mathbf{a}))=H_d(\mathbf{a})^{\eta_n}\). For a general atom, remove one largest leg dimension and apply the same formula to the remaining dimensions. This assignment is invariant under permutations of the legs. For _n_=3, it recovers the symmetric certificate of \[ABZ26, Equation (5.3)\]. The factors in _Hd_ are chosen to handle both changes of input length and changes of their sorted order. Within each fixed order, differentiation proves monotonicity and concavity in each coordinate. When two entries cross, the first derivatives agree. Thus the same properties hold across all sorting intervals. Once one coordinate exceeds the others, _Hd_ is affine in that coordinate, with the offset needed for shifted tripling. Lemma 5.8 proves these facts, together with \(H_d(\mathbf{a})\le\prod_{i=1}^da_i,H_d(\mathbf{a})^{\eta_n}\le 1+\sum_{i=1}^d(a_i-1).\) The first bound accounts for the rule that constructs a polynomial tensor from a star of edge tensors; the second accounts for interpolation. Concavity and shifted tripling give the

## 2 Preliminaries

In this section, we define the tensor operations and the asymptotic parameters used in the proof. Our spectral framework is the asymptotic spectrum theory developed by Strassen \[Str88, Section 3\]; Wigderson and Zuiddam \[WZ26\] give a detailed account of its semiring formulation, applications, and extensions. We first specify tensor arrays and their coordinate operations. We then identify arrays that differ only by independent coordinate permutations within their legs, define the resulting tensor semiring, and introduce the asymptotic parameters and graph tensors. Unless a coefficient semiring R is explicitly specified, all tensors are over C.

We write N={0,1,2_,..._} and \[_q_\]<sub>0</sub>={0_,...,q_-1} for every positive integer _q_. All coordinate indices start at 0. We use log for the logarithm to base 2 and ln for the natural logarithm. For a positive integer _s_, a _probability vector_ is a vector \(\theta=(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_s)\) with \(\theta_h\ge 0\) for \(1\le h\le s\) and \(\sum_{h=1}^s\theta_h=1\). Its entropy is

\(H(\theta)=-\sum_{h=1}^s\theta_h\mathrm{ln}\theta_h,\)

where 0ln0=0. Thus entropy factors below take the form \(e^{H(\theta)}\).

### 2.1 Tensor coordinates and operations

We begin with coordinate operations, and then specify which coordinate choices are identified. The distinction matters when several tensor blocks share a leg.

**Definition 2.1** (tensor arrays)**.** Let R be a commutative semiring: (R,+<sub>R</sub>,0<sub>R</sub>) and \((\mathcal{R},\cdot_\mathcal{R},1_\mathcal{R})\) are commutative monoids, multiplication distributes over addition, \(0_\mathcal{R}\cdot_\mathcal{R}x=0_\mathcal{R}\) for all \(x\in\mathcal{R}\), and \(1_\mathcal{R}\neq 0_\mathcal{R}\). For positive integers _k,n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>_, a _k-th order tensor array_ of dimension (_n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>_) over R is a function

\(T:[n_1]_0\times\cdots\times[n_k]_0\longrightarrow\mathcal{R}.\)

We write _T_<sub>_i_<sub>1</sub>_,...,i<sub>k</sub>_</sub> for its value at (_i_<sub>1</sub>_,...,i<sub>k</sub>_) and set dim(_T_)=(_n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>_). The _d_-th index, for \(1\le d\le k\), is called the _d_-th _leg_. Let Arr_<sub>k</sub>_(R) be the disjoint union of these array spaces over all positive dimension vectors. When R=C, we call its elements _complex k-th order tensor arrays_. An array is nonzero if its support is nonempty.

For \(A,B\in\mathsf{Arr}_k(\mathcal{R})\) with the same dimension (_n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>_) and \(c\in\mathcal{R}\), define their _entrywise sum_ and scalar multiple by<tbc>

\((A+B)_{i_1,\dots,i_k}=A_{i_1,\dots,i_k}+_\mathcal{R}B_{i_1,\dots,i_k},(cA)_{i_1,\dots,i_k}=c\cdot_\mathcal{R}A_{i_1,\dots,i_k}\)

<tbc>for \(0\le i_d<n_d\) and \(1\le d\le k\). The _support_ of _T_ is<tbc>

\(\mathrm{supp}(T)=\big\{(i_1,\dots,i_k)\in[n_1]_0\times\cdots\times[n_k]_0:T_{i_1,\dots,i_k}\neq 0_\mathcal{R}\big\}.\)

The entrywise sum is different from the direct sum defined next. We retain the subscript _K_ in both operations that preserve tensor order.

**Definition 2.2** (Kronecker direct sum and product)**.** Let _k_ be a positive integer, and let \(A,B\in\mathsf{Arr}_k(\mathcal{R})\) have dimensions (_n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>_) and (_m_<sub>1</sub>_,...,m<sub>k</sub>_), respectively. Their _Kronecker direct sum_ \(A\oplus_KB\) has dimension (_n_<sub>1</sub>+_m_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>+m<sub>k</sub>_) and entries<tbc>

\((A\oplus_KB)_{u_1,\dots,u_k}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
A_{u_1,\dots,u_k}, & 0\le u_d<n_d\text{for}1\le d\le k, \\
B_{u_1-n_1,\dots,u_k-n_k}, & n_d\le u_d<n_d+m_d\text{for}1\le d\le k, \\
0_\mathcal{R}, & \text{otherwise,}
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>for \(0\le u_d<n_d+m_d\) and \(1\le d\le k\). Their _Kronecker product_ \(A\otimes_KB\) has dimension (_n_<sub>1</sub>_m_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>m<sub>k</sub>_) and entries<tbc>

\((A\otimes_KB)_{i_1m_1+j_1,\dots,i_km_k+j_k}=A_{i_1,\dots,i_k}\cdot_\mathcal{R}B_{j_1,\dots,j_k}\)

<tbc>for \(0\le i_d<n_d\), \(0\le j_d<m_d\), and \(1\le d\le k\). For every positive integer _r_, write

\(A^{\oplus_Kr}=\oplus_Kh=1^rA,A^{\otimes_Kr}=\otimes_Kh=1^rA\)

for the repeated direct sum and repeated Kronecker product, respectively. Repeated operations on distinct arrays use their displayed order.

**Definition 2.3** (tensor construction)**.** Let _p,q_ be positive integers. For arrays \(A\in\mathsf{Arr}_p(\mathcal{R})\) and \(B\in\mathsf{Arr}_q(\mathcal{R})\) with dimensions (_n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>p</sub>_) and (_m_<sub>1</sub>_,...,m<sub>q</sub>_), define \(A\otimes_CB\in\mathsf{Arr}_{p+q}(\mathcal{R})\) by<tbc>

\((A\otimes_CB)_{i_1,\dots,i_p,j_1,\dots,j_q}=A_{i_1,\dots,i_p}\cdot_\mathcal{R}B_{j_1,\dots,j_q}\)

<tbc>for \(0\le i_d<n_d\) and \(1\le d\le p\), and for \(0\le j_d<m_d\) and \(1\le d\le q\). For every positive integer _q_ and \(d\in[q]_0\), let \(e_d^{(q)}\) be the first-order tensor array of dimension (_q_) with entries \((e_d^{(q)})_i=1_\mathcal{R}\) if _i=d_ and 0<sub>R</sub> otherwise, for \(i\in[q]_0\). For positive integers _k,q_, define the _diagonal tensor array_

\(\mathsf{l}_k(q)=\sum_{d=0}^{q-1}\otimes_{h=1}^ke_d^{(q)}.\)

Thus dim(l_<sub>k</sub>(q_))=(_q,...,q_) and \(\mathsf{l}_k(q)=\mathsf{l}_k(1)^{\oplus_Kq}\) as arrays. The notation l_<sub>k</sub>_(0) will be defined after we introduce the tensor semiring.

**Definition 2.4** (local maps and restriction)**.** Let _k_ be a positive integer. Let \(T,S\in\mathsf{Arr}_k(\mathcal{R})\) have dimensions (_n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>_) and (_m_<sub>1</sub>_,...,m<sub>k</sub>_), respectively. Given matrices \(L_d\in\mathcal{R}^{m_d\times n_d}\) for \(1\le d\le k\), put _L_=(_L_<sub>1</sub>_,...,L<sub>k</sub>_) and define

\((L\cdot T)_{j_1,\dots,j_k}=\sum_{0\le i_d<n_d1\le d\le k}T_{i_1,\dots,i_k}\prod_{d=1}^k(L_d)_{j_d,i_d}\)

for \(0\le j_d<m_d\) and \(1\le d\le k\). We say that _S_ is a _restriction_ of _T_, and write \(S\unknown T\) or \(T\unknown S\), if \(S=L\cdot T\) for some such matrices. We write \(S\cong T\) if their dimensions agree and the matrices can be chosen invertible. Finally, write _S∼T_ if \(S\unknown T\) and \(T\unknown S\).

**Definition 2.5** (coordinate-permutation equivalence)**.** Let _k_ be a positive integer, and let \(A,B\in\mathsf{Arr}_k(\mathcal{R})\). Write \(A\equiv_\mathrm{perm}B\) if dim(_A_)=dim(_B_)=(_n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>_) and there are permutations \(\sigma_d:[n_d]_0\rightarrow[n_d]_0\), for \(1\le d\le k\), such that

\(B_{i_1,\dots,i_k}=A_{\sigma_1(i_1),\dots,\sigma_k(i_k)}\)

for \(0\le i_d<n_d\) and \(1\le d\le k\). The permutations act independently within the legs; they do not exchange the legs. Identity permutations, inverse permutations, and composition show that \(\equiv_\mathrm{perm}\) is an equivalence relation.

**Definition 2.6** (tensors and the tensor semiring)**.** Let _k_ be a positive integer. For this definition, assume that R has no zero divisors: for all \(x,y\in\mathcal{R}\), the equality _xy_=0<sub>R</sub> implies _x_=0<sub>R</sub> or _y_=0<sub>R</sub>. Let \(\mathsf{Arr}_k^\times(\mathcal{R})\) be the set of nonzero arrays in Arr_<sub>k</sub>_(R), and put<tbc>

\(\mathsf{Tens}_k(\mathcal{R})=\left(\mathsf{Arr}_k^\times(\mathcal{R})/\equiv_\mathrm{perm}\right)\sqcup\{0_k\},\)

<tbc>where 0_<sub>k</sub>_ is a new formal element. An element of Tens_<sub>k</sub>_(R) is a _k-th order tensor over_ R; when R=C, it is a _complex k-th order tensor_. For nonzero classes, define

\([A]\oplus_K\left[B\right]=[A\oplus_KB],[A]\otimes_K\left[B\right]=[A\otimes_KB].\)

Extend these operations by \(T\oplus_K0_k=0_k\oplus_KT=T\) and \(T\otimes_K0_k=0_k\otimes_KT=0_k\) for every \(T\in\mathsf{Tens}_k(\mathcal{R})\). The unit is the class of l_<sub>k</sub>_(1), and we set l_<sub>k</sub>_(0)=0_<sub>k</sub>_. We use the same notation for a nonzero array and its class, and write 0 for 0_<sub>k</sub>_ when the order is clear. For every tensor _T_, set \(T^{\oplus_K0}=0_k\) and \(T^{\otimes_K0}=\mathsf{l}_k(1)\).

The extra assumption on R is used only to construct this semiring and holds in particular for C. It ensures that a product of two nonzero arrays is nonzero. The array definitions themselves apply to every commutative coefficient semiring. Our use of coordinate-permutation classes follows Wigderson and Zuiddam \[WZ26, Example 2.20\]; we explicitly adjoin the zero element, as permitted by their semiring convention \[WZ26, Definition 2.1\].

We verify the semiring properties. Permutations on _A_ and _B_ combine into a block permutation on each leg of \(A\oplus_KB\). For \(A\otimes_KB\), the permutations on leg _d_ act on the paired index by \((i,j)\mapsto(\sigma_d(i),\tau_d(j))\). Thus both operations are independent of the representatives. Associativity follows by concatenating three coordinate blocks for direct sums and by identifying the three paired indices for products. Swapping the two blocks on every leg proves commutativity of \(\oplus_K\). The permutation \(im_d+j\mapsto jn_d+i\) on leg _d_ proves commutativity of \(\otimes_K\).

For distributivity, the coordinates on each leg of \(A\otimes_K\left(B\oplus_KC\right)\) have the form (_i,j_) with _j_ in either the _B_ block or the _C_ block. List the pairs from the _B_ block first and those from the _C_ block second. This gives the coordinate order of \((A\otimes_KB)\oplus_K\left(A\otimes_KC\right)\). Terms choosing different blocks on different legs have coefficient zero on both sides, and the remaining coefficients agree by the definition of \(\otimes_K\). Hence distributivity also holds. The class of l_<sub>k</sub>_(1) is a multiplicative unit. Finally, all identities involving 0_<sub>k</sub>_ follow from its defining rules. Therefore Tens_<sub>k</sub>_(R) is a commutative semiring.

**Remark 2.7** (coordinates and tensor relations)**.** For a nonzero tensor, its dimension vector is the common dimension vector of its representatives. The formal zero tensor has no fixed positive dimension vector. In a coordinate identity, it is written as the zero coefficient table of the stated ambient dimensions. This convention is used for entrywise sums and local maps, not to replace the defining rules for \(\oplus_K\) and \(\otimes_K\) involving 0_<sub>k</sub>_.

The operation \(\otimes_C\) also descends to nonzero classes, because coordinate permutations of its factors act on disjoint groups of legs. For \(S\in\mathsf{Tens}_p(\mathcal{R})\) and \(T\in\mathsf{Tens}_q(\mathcal{R})\), set \(0_p\otimes_CT=\)<tbc>

\(S\otimes_C0_q=0_{p+q}\). Scalar multiplication descends in the same way, with scalar zero giving the formal zero tensor.

The relations \(\unknown\), \(\cong\), and ∼ descend to nonzero tensors: changing input and output representatives only composes their local maps with permutation matrices. Extend them by \(0_k\unknown T\) for every _T_, by \(T\unknown 0_k\) only for _T_=0_<sub>k</sub>_, and by \(0_k\cong 0_k\). Thus ∼ still means mutual restriction and is not the equivalence used to define tensors. In particular, adding zero coordinates can change a tensor, although it gives a mutually restricting tensor.

Entrywise addition and the action of a specified local matrix require chosen, aligned coordinates. For example, \((1,0)\equiv_\mathrm{perm}(0,1)\), but (1,0)+(1,0)=(2,0) and (1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1) are not coordinate-permutation equivalent over C. Throughout the paper, a formula for tensor entries, an entrywise sum, or a local substitution uses the displayed coordinate representatives. The labels in \(e_d^{(q)}\) refer to those coordinates. With this convention, coordinate calculations describe tensors without identifying them under arbitrary invertible local maps or under mutual restriction.

**Remark 2.8** (tensor construction and Kronecker product)**.** The operation \(\otimes_C\) concatenates the legs, whereas \(\otimes_K\) pairs corresponding legs and retains their number. For example, over C, the tensor \(e_0^{(2)}\otimes_Ce_0^{(2)}+e_1^{(2)}\otimes_Ce_1^{(2)}\) is a second-order tensor of rank 2, whereas

\(e_0^{(2)}\otimes_Ke_0^{(2)}+e_1^{(2)}\otimes_Ke_1^{(2)}=(1,0,0,1)\)

is a nonzero first-order tensor of rank 1. Tensor rank, defined in Definition 2.12, is invariant under invertible changes of coordinates within each fixed leg. It need not be invariant under regrouping the legs. Our notation records this distinction.

The separation construction uses a partial direct sum: two legs have separate coordinates for each block, while the other legs use the same coordinates. The following definition makes these shared coordinates part of the data.

**Definition 2.9** (partial direct sum in aligned coordinates)**.** Let \(k\ge 2\) and \(M\ge 1\) be integers, and let _e_=(_u,v_) with \(1\le u<v\le k\). For \(0\le h<M\), let _T<sub>h</sub>_ be a complex _k_-th order tensor in specified coordinates of positive ambient dimensions (_n_<sub>1_,h_</sub>_,...,n<sub>k,h</sub>_). Assume that _n<sub>d,h</sub>=n<sub>d</sub>_ for every \(d\notin\{u,v\}\) and every \(0\le h<M\), and identify these coordinates in the displayed order. Put<tbc>

\(\beta_h=\sum_{t=0}^{h-1}n_{u,t},\gamma_h=\sum_{t=0}^{h-1}n_{v,t}(0\le h\le M),\)

<tbc>where the sums are empty when _h_=0. Define \(m_u=\beta_M\), \(m_v=\gamma_M\), and _m<sub>d</sub>=n<sub>d</sub>_ for \(d\notin\{u,v\}\). For \(1\le d\le k\) and \(0\le h<M\), let<tbc>

\(\eta_{d,h}=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\beta_h, & d=u, \\
\gamma_h, & d=v, \\
0, & d\notin\{u,v\}.
\end{array}\right.\)

<tbc>The _partial direct sum_ \(A=T_0\boxplus_e\cdots\boxplus_et_{M-1}\) is specified in ambient dimensions (_m_<sub>1</sub>_,...,m<sub>k</sub>_) by

\(A_{i_1+\eta_{1,h},\dots,i_k+\eta_{k,h}}=(T_h)_{i_1,\dots,i_k}\)

The sectors assigned to different _h_ are disjoint: the _u_-th coordinate lies in \([\beta_h,\beta_{h+1})\) and the _v_-th coordinate lies in \([\gamma_h,\gamma_{h+1})\). In particular, entries<tbc>

using different sectors on the two legs are zero. A zero block uses the zero coefficient table in its specified ambient dimensions. **Definition 2.10** (formal multilinear notation)**.** Let _k,n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>_ be positive integers, and let _T_ be a complex _k_-th order tensor in specified coordinates of dimensions (_n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>_). Introduce distinct commuting indeterminates \(x_i^{(d)}\) for \(1\le d\le k\) and \(0\le i<n_d\). The _formal multilinear expression_ of _T_ in these coordinates is<tbc>

<tbc>For positive integers _m_<sub>1</sub>_,...,m<sub>k</sub>_ and matrices \(L_d\in\mathbb{C}^{m_d\times n_d}\) for \(1\le d\le k\), the local map _L_=(_L_<sub>1</sub>_,...,L<sub>k</sub>_) is represented by the substitutions

\(x_i^{(d)}\longmapsto\sum_{j=0}^{m_d-1}(L_d)_{j,i}y_j^{(d)}(1\le d\le k,0\le i<n_d),\)

where the \(y_j^{(d)}\) are distinct commuting output indeterminates. Expanding gives the formal multilinear expression of \(L\cdot T\) from Definition 2.4.

A product of symbols records one basis tensor and keeps the _k_ legs separate. This notation lets us specify local maps by their action on coordinate symbols and read their effect on the supported terms. We use it for simultaneous separation in Theorem 3.1, the two polynomial constructions in Lemmas 4.8 and 4.9, and the local weights in the proof of Theorem B.4.

**Definition 2.11** (permutations of tensor legs)**.** For every positive integer _k_, let _S<sub>k</sub>_ be the set of permutations of {1_,...,k_}. For \(\pi\in S_k\) and a nonzero complex _k_-th order tensor _T_ of dimension (_n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>_), define \(\pi T\) by the dimensions \((n_{\pi^{-1}(1)},\dots,n_{\pi^{-1}(k)})\) and the coordinate formula

\((\pi T)_{j_1,\dots,j_k}=T_{j_{\pi(1)},\dots,j_{\pi(k)}}\)

A change of representative for _T_ induces a change of representative for \(\pi T\), so this action is well-defined. Thus old leg _d_ becomes new leg \(\pi(d)\). This operation permutes the participants, whereas \(\equiv_\mathrm{perm}\) only permutes coordinates within each fixed leg.

## 2.2 Asymptotic rank and the spectrum

We now use local maps to define rank and subrank, and then describe their behavior under large Kronecker powers. Strassen’s spectral duality will provide the link between these tensor parameters and the numerical inequalities in our proof.

**Definition 2.12** (rank and subrank)**.** For a positive integer _k_ and a complex _k_-th order tensor _T_, its _rank_ is \(\mathrm{R}(T)=\mathrm{min}\{r\in\mathbb{N}:T\unknown\mathsf{I}_k(r)\}\). For \(k\ge 2\), its _subrank_ is \(\mathrm{Q}(T)=\mathrm{max}\{q\in\mathbb{N}:\mathsf{I}_k(q)\unknown T\}\). Equivalently, fix coordinates of dimensions (_n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>k</sub>_) for _T_. Then R(_T_) is the smallest nonnegative integer _r_ for which

\(T=\sum_{h=1}^r\otimes_{d=1}^kv_{d,h},v_{d,h}\in\mathbb{C}^{n_d}(1\le d\le k,1\le h\le r).\)

An empty sum denotes the zero coefficient table in these coordinates. A tensor of the form \(\otimes_{Cd=1}^kv_d\), with \(v_d\in\mathbb{C}^{n_d}\) for \(1\le d\le k\), is called a _simple tensor_. The rank of the zero tensor is 0; for \(k\ge 2\), its subrank is also 0.

For \(r\ge 1\), the two definitions of rank agree by taking the vectors _v<sub>d,h</sub>_ as the columns of the local maps from I_<sub>k</sub>(r_); the case _r_=0 follows from the conventions for the zero tensor. The standard basis expansion is a finite sum of simple tensors, so every tensor has finite rank. A nonzero tensor restricts to I_<sub>k</sub>_(1) by selecting one nonzero entry and rescaling it. For \(k\ge 2\) and nonzero _T_, we also have \(\mathrm{Q}(T)\le\mathrm{min}_{1\le d\le k}n_d\): grouping leg_d_ against all other legs gives a matrix of rank at most _n<sub>d</sub>_, while the corresponding matrix of I_<sub>k</sub>(q_) has rank _q_. Local maps cannot increase this matrix rank. The general statement about such _flattenings_ is defined and proved in Definition A.1 and Lemma A.2. Hence the maximum defining subrank exists. Composing restrictions also shows that rank and subrank are unchanged under ∼.

**Definition 2.13** (asymptotic rank and subrank)**.** For every integer \(k\ge 2\) and every nonzero complex _k_-th order tensor _T_, define

## 4 Polynomial Multiplication and the Complete Graph Bound

We now use the entropy inequality to prove the complete graph bound. The proof compares two estimates for a symmetric spectral profile of polynomial multiplication: interpolation gives an upper bound, while two degenerations force growth as the input lengths increase. We first define the tensors and their profiles, then establish discrete concavity and shifted tripling. A coordinate-by-coordinate growth argument will turn these inequalities into the upper bound of Theorem 1.1.

**Lemma 4.2** (rank of polynomial multiplication)**.** _For every integer_ \(n\ge 3\) _and all positive integers a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-1</sub>,<tbc>

\(\mathrm{R}\big(\mathcal{C}_n(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})\big)=1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(a_j-1).\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Put \(D=1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(a_j-1)\), and choose distinct complex numbers \(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_D\). For every integer \(1\le r\le D\), let<tbc>

\(L_r(x)=\prod_{1\le s\le Ds\neq r}\frac{x-\xi_s}{\xi_r-\xi_s},\)

<tbc>and let \(c_r\in\mathbb{C}^D\) be its coefficient vector, in increasing order of degree. Lagrange interpolation states that every polynomial _f_ of degree at most _D_-1 satisfies \(f(x)=\sum_{r=1}^Df(\xi_r)L_r(x)\). Apply this identity to \(f=\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}f_j\), whose degree is at most _D_-1. For \(1\le j\le n-1\) and \(1\le r\le D\), define the evaluation vector<tbc>

\(v_{j,r}=\sum_{i=0}^{a_j-1}\xi_r^ie_i^{(a_j)}.\)

The interpolation identity holds for every choice of the input coefficients. Equating their coefficients therefore gives the tensor identity

\(\mathcal{C}_n(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})=\sum_{r=1}^Dv_{1,r}\otimes_C\cdots\otimes_Cv_{n-1,r}\otimes_Cc_r.\)

This is a sum of _D_ simple tensors, so the rank is at most _D_.

For the reverse inequality, flatten the output leg against all input legs, as in Definition A.1. For every integer \(0\le s<D\), row _s_ has entry 1 precisely at the input tuples with \(i_1+\cdots+i_{n-1}=s\). Such a tuple exists for every _s_: the sum of the integer intervals \[_a<sub>j</sub>_\]<sub>0</sub>, for \(1\le j\le n-1\), is the integer interval \[_D_\]<sub>0</sub>. To see this directly, the sum of {0_,...,r_} and {0_,...,t_} is {0_,...,r+t_}, since an integer _s_ in the latter interval can be written as min{_s,r_}+(_s_-min{_s,r_}). Repeatedly applying this observation proves the claim about the input intervals.

Thus every row is nonzero. Different rows have disjoint supports, because an input tuple has a unique coordinate sum. The _D_ rows are therefore linearly independent. The flattening has matrix rank _D_, and every simple tensor has flattening rank at most one. Hence the tensor rank is at least _D_, proving equality.

We next attach one number to each pair of tensor legs. These numbers depend on a chosen spectral point. They are distinct from the graph edge exponent \(\tau(G)\) in Definition 2.22, which is defined using asymptotic rank itself.

**Definition 4.3** (spectral edge weights)**.** Let \(n\ge 2\) be an integer, and let \(\phi\in\Phi_n\). For every pair of integers \(1\le i<j\le n\), define

\(p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}=log_2\phi(E_{i,j}^{(2)}).\)

Here \(E_{i,j}^{(2)}\) is the complex _n_-th order edge tensor from Definition 2.20: only legs _i_ and _j_ have dimension greater than one. We call \(p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}\) its _spectral edge weight under_ \(\phi\).

The next lemma extends the single-edge calculation in \[Ope26a, Section 2\]. It shows that this weight determines the spectral value for every edge dimension, not only dimension two.

**Lemma 4.4** (spectral edge weights)**.** _Let_ \(n\ge 2\) _be an integer, let_ \(\phi\in\Phi_n\)_, and let_ \(p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}\) _be as in Definition 4.3. For all integers_ \(1\le i<j\le n\) _and_ \(q\ge 1\)_, we have_ \(0\le p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}\le 1\) _and_ \(\phi(E_{i,j}^{(q)})=q^{p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}}\)_. Moreover,_

\(\sum_{j=2}^np_{1,j}^{(\phi)}\ge 1,\phi(\mathsf{GT}_q(K_n))=q^{\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}}(q\ge 1).\)

_Proof._ Fix integers \(1\le i<j\le n\), and set \(f(q)=\phi(E_{i,j}^{(q)})\) for every positive integer _q_. If \(q\le r\), projecting the two nontrivial legs onto their first _q_ coordinates restricts \(E_{i,j}^{(r)}\) to \(E_{i,j}^{(q)}\). Thus _f_ is nondecreasing. For all positive integers _q,r_, the local pairing of the edge labels gives \(E_{i,j}^{(q)}\otimes_KE_{i,j}^{(r)}\cong E_{i,j}^{(qr)}\), so _f(qr_)=_f(q)f(r_). The tensor \(E_{i,j}^{(q)}\) is nonzero and has rank _q_: its defining sum has _q_ terms, and its flattening across leg _i_ has rank _q_. Hence \(1\le f(q)\le q\), which in particular proves \(0\le p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}=log_2f(2)\le 1\).

Let \(q\ge 2\) be an integer. For every positive integer _N_, put \(\ell_N=\lfloor Nlog_2q\rfloor\). Since \(2^{\ell_N}\le q^N<2^{\ell_N+1}\), monotonicity and multiplicativity give<tbc>

\(f(2)^{\ell_N}\le f(q)^N\le f(2)^{\ell_N+1}.\)

Taking logarithms and dividing by _N_ yields

\(\frac{\ell_N}{N}p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}\le\mathrm{log}_2f(q)\le\frac{\ell_N+1}{N}p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}.\)

Both outer expressions tend to \(p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}\mathrm{log}_2q\). Therefore \(f(q)=q^{p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}}\). For _q_=1, the formula follows from \(E_{i,j}^{(1)}=\mathsf{l}_n(1)\).

Consider the star tensor \(T=\otimes_{K_{j=2}}^nE_{1,j}^{(2)}\). At its first leg, a basis vector is indexed by a tuple \((b_2,\dots,b_n)\in\{0,1\}^{n-1}\). Apply the linear map sending this vector to \(e_b^{(2)}\) if \(b_2=\cdots=b_n=b\), and to zero otherwise. At leg _j_, for \(2\le j\le n\), leave the coordinate _b<sub>j</sub>_ unchanged. The surviving terms are exactly the two terms of l_<sub>n</sub>_(2). Restriction monotonicity and multiplicativity now imply

\(2=\phi(\mathsf{l}_n(2))\le\phi(T)=\prod_{j=2}^n\phi(E_{1,j}^{(2)})=2^{\sum_{j=2}^np_{1,j}^{(\phi)}}.\)

Taking logarithms proves the first inequality. Finally, \(\mathsf{GT}_q(K_n)=\otimes_{K_{1\le i<j\le n}}E_{i,j}^{(q)}\) by Definition 2.20. Applying multiplicativity and the edge formula proves the asserted value on the complete graph.

We now average over all permutations of the _n_ tensor legs. This extends the six-factor symmetrization used in \[Ope26a, Equation (4.4)\].

**Definition 4.5** (symmetric spectral profile)**.** Let \(n\ge 3\) be an integer, let \(\phi\in\Phi_n\), and let \(p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}\) be its spectral edge weights. Define their average by<tbc>

\(m=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2},t_\phi=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}.\)

<tbc>For every permutation \(\pi\in S_n\), put \(\phi_\pi(T)=\phi(\pi T)\), where the action on tensor legs is defined in Section 2. For all positive integers _a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-1</sub>, define the _symmetric spectral profile_

\(P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})=\left(\prod_{\pi\in S_n}\phi_\pi\big(\mathcal{C}_n(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})\big)\right)^{1/(n!t_\phi)}.\)

Lemma 4.4 gives \(t_\phi\ge 1/m>0\), so the definition uses a positive exponent. Every map \(\phi_\pi\) is a spectral point: permutation of the legs preserves restriction, the diagonal tensors, and both semiring operations.

For integers \(1\le u<v\le n\) and \(\pi\in S_n\), Definition 4.3 gives \(p_{u,v}^{(\phi_\pi)}=\mathrm{log}_2\phi_\pi(E_{u,v}^{(2)})\). The image of the pair (_u,v_) under \(\pi\) is the pair \((\mathrm{min}(\pi(u),\pi(v)),\mathrm{max}(\pi(u),\pi(v)))\). For any fixed pair \(1\le i<j\le n\), exactly 2(_n_-2)! permutations send (_u,v_) to (_i,j_) in this sense: there are two choices for the images of _u,v_, and (_n_-2)! choices for the remaining images. Consequently,<tbc>

\(\sum_{\pi\in S_n}p_{u,v}^{(\phi_\pi)}=2(n-2)!\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}=n!t_\phi(1\le u<v\le n).\) (2)

<tbc>**Lemma 4.6** (basic properties of the profile)**.** _For every integer_ \(n\ge 3\) _and every spectral point_ \(\phi\in\Phi_n\)_, the profile in Definition 4.5 is positive and symmetric in its n_-1 _arguments. For every positive integer b and all positive integers a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-1</sub>_, it satisfies_<tbc>

\(P_\phi(1,\dots,1,b)=b,P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})\le\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(a_j-1)\right)^{1/t_\phi}.\)

_Proof._ Every polynomial multiplication tensor is nonzero, and a spectral point has value at least one on a nonzero tensor. Thus each factor in the definition of \(P_\phi\) is positive, and so is \(P_\phi\).

Let \(\sigma\) permute the first _n_-1 tensor legs and fix leg _n_. By the defining coefficient formula, permuting the input lengths of C_<sub>n</sub>_ by \(\sigma\) gives \(\sigma\mathcal{C}_n\). The map \(\pi\mapsto\pi\sigma\) is a bijection of _S<sub>n</sub>_. Hence replacing C_<sub>n</sub>_ by \(\sigma\mathcal{C}_n\) reindexes the factors defining \(P_\phi\) and does not change their product. This proves symmetry.

The tensor \(\mathcal{C}_n(1,\dots,1,b)\) equals \(E_{n-1,n}^{(b)}\). Using (2), we obtain<tbc>

\(P_\phi(1,\dots,1,b)=\left(\prod_{\pi\in S_n}b_{n-1,n}^{p_{n-1,n}^{(\phi_\pi)}}\right)^{1/(n!t_\phi)}=b.\)

<tbc>For the upper bound, a spectral point is at most tensor rank, and tensor rank is unchanged by a permutation of the legs. Thus Lemma 4.2 gives, for every \(\pi\in S_n\),

\(\phi_\pi\big(\mathcal{C}_n(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})\big)\le 1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}(a_j-1).\)

There are _n_! factors in the profile. Multiplying their bounds and then taking the power \(1/(n!t_\phi)\) proves the result.

**Remark 4.7.** The profile \(P_\phi\) is a numerical function of input lengths. The geometric mean defining it is not asserted to be a spectral point. In the next two subsections, every tensor comparison is applied separately to each \(\phi_\pi\); only the resulting numerical inequalities are multiplied together.

## 4.2 Discrete concavity

The first comparison concerns three consecutive values of one input length. We will retain a quotient part and a kernel part of a doubled multiplication tensor. Both parts use the same coordinates on the first _n_-2 input legs, so Corollary 3.2 applies to them. This construction and the shifted tripling construction in Subsection 4.3 extend the determinant filtration and three-sector decomposition of OpenAI \[Ope26a, Section 4\]. Averaging their spectral inequalities over all leg permutations gives inequalities for the profile from Subsection 4.1.

The following inequality extends \[Ope26a, Lemma 4.1\]. We give the coordinate action of the kernel and quotient maps explicitly, so that their compatibility with every tuple of shared inputs can be checked without combining those inputs into one leg.

**Lemma 4.8** (discrete concavity)**.** _Let_ \(n\ge 3\) _be an integer, let_ \(\phi\in\Phi_n\)_, and let_ \(P_\phi\) _be the profile in Definition 4.5. For all positive integers a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-2</sub> _and every integer_ \(b\ge 2\),

\(2P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},b)\ge P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},b+1)+P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},b-1).\)

_By symmetry, the same inequality holds in every input coordinate._

_Proof._ Put \(S=\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}(a_j-1)\). For every integer \(e\ge 0\), let _V<sub>e</sub>_ be the vector space of homogeneous polynomials of degree _e_ in the variables _u,v_, with ordered basis \((u^{e-i}v^i)_{i=0}^e\). The coefficient vector of \(\sum_{i=0}^ec_ix^i\) is thus also the coefficient vector of \(\sum_{i=0}^ec_iu^{e-i}v^i\). Multiplication of these homogeneous forms has the same coefficient tensor as univariate polynomial multiplication.

Let _s,w_ be two more variables. For every integer \(e\ge 0\), define \(U_e=\{Fs+Gw:F,G\in V_e\}.\) We use the ordered basis _u__e-i__vis,u__e-i__viw_, first in increasing _i_ and then in the displayed order within each pair. The tensor \(\mathcal{C}_n(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},b)\otimes_KE_{n-1,n}^{(2)}\) represents the multilinear map \(V_{a_1-1}\times\cdots\times V_{a_{n-2}-1}\times U_{b-1}\longrightarrow U_{S+b-1},\)
\((f_1,\dots,f_{n-2},F)\longmapsto\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}f_j\right)F.\) Indeed, the edge tensor preserves the choice of _s_ or _w_ from the last input to the output, while C_n_ multiplies the coefficient polynomials. This changes only the indexing of the last two legs. The other _n_-2 inputs remain separate legs. We now construct bases of the last input and output spaces that work for every choice of the shared inputs. Put _D=uw-vs_. For every integer \(e\ge 1\), define the linear map \(\rho_e:U_e\longrightarrow V_{e+1},\rho_e(Fs+Gw)=uF+vG.\) For integers \(0\le i\le e\), put _qe,i=u__e-i__vis_, and put _q__e,e_+1=_vew_. Their images under \(\rho_e\) are, in order, all the monomials _u__e_+1-_i__vi_ with \(0\le i\le e+1\). Hence \(\rho_e\) is surjective. Multiplication by _D_ is injective on _V__e_-1, since _D_ is nonzero and the polynomial ring C\[_u,v,s,w_\] has no zero divisors. Also, \(\rho_e(Dg)=0\) for every \(g\in V_{e-1}\). The kernel has dimension (2_e_+2)-(_e_+2)=_e_, which equals dim_V__e_-1. Thus multiplication by _D_ identifies _V__e_-1 with the entire kernel, giving the exact sequence \(0\longrightarrow V_{e-1}-\rightarrow^{g\mapsto Dg}U_e-\rightarrow^{\rho_e}V_{e+1}\longrightarrow 0.\) In particular, an ordered basis of _Ue_ consists of the vectors _q__e,_0_,...,q__e,e_+1, followed by \(k_{e,j}=Du^{e-1-j}v^j(0\le je,i_ vanish because their images form a basis of _V__e_+1. Injectivity of multiplication by _D_ then forces the coefficients of all _ke,j_ to vanish. There are (_e_+2)+_e_=2_e_+2=dim_Ue_ vectors, so they form a basis. Use these bases with _e=b_-1 and _e=S+b_-1. Both are at least one because \(b\ge 2\) and \(S\ge 0\). Fix any tuple of shared input forms \(f_j\in V_{a_j-1}\), for \(1\le j\le n-2\), and put \(f=\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}f_j\in V_S\). Multiplication by _f_ respects both the quotient and the kernel: \(\rho_{S+b-1}(fF)=f\rho_{b-1}(F)(F\in U_{b-1}),\)
\(f(Dg)=D(fg)(g\in V_{b-2}).\) We spell out what these two identities say about the coefficients. Write \(f=\sum_{t=0}^Sc_tu^{S-t}v^t,c_t=0(t\in\mathbb{Z}\backslash\{0,\dots,S\}).\) For an input quotient lift _q__b_-1_,i_, where \(0\le i\le b\), its image under \(\rho_{b-1}\) is _u__b-i__vi_. Thus the output quotient coordinates of _fq__b_-1_,i_ are _c__r-i_ for \(0\le r\le S+b\). Subtracting the corresponding

quotient lifts leaves an element of the output kernel. There are consequently unique complex coefficients \(\eta_{r,i}(f)\), for \(0\le r\le S+b-2\) and \(0\le i\le b\), such that

\(fq_{b-1,i}=\sum_{r=0}^{S+b}c_{r-i}q_{S+b-1,r}+\sum_{r=0}^{S+b-2}\eta_{r,i}(f)k_{S+b-1,r}(0\le i\le b),fk_{b-1,j}=\sum_{r=0}^{S+b-2}c_{r-j}k_{S+b-1,r}(0\le j\le b-2).\text{(3)}\)

The second equality follows by expanding _fDu_<sup>_b_-2-_j_</sup>_v<sup>j</sup>_. In particular, a kernel input has no quotient output. A quotient input can have a kernel output, and the coefficients \(\eta_{r,i}(f)\) record precisely those terms.

The chosen input and output bases depend only on _b_ and _S_. They do not depend on _f_, or on its factorization as \(\prod_{j=1}^{n-2}f_j\). Therefore (3) holds simultaneously for every choice of basis vector on each of the first _n_-2 input legs. The two basis changes are invertible local maps on the last input and output legs; no shared leg is changed. On the input leg, the coefficient tensor uses the dual of the basis-change matrix, which is again invertible.

Assign weight zero to all shared coordinates and quotient coordinates. Assign weight -1 to the last-input kernel coordinates and weight +1 to the output kernel coordinates. Every term in the first sum of (3) has total weight zero. Every term involving \(\eta_{r,i}(f)\) has weight +1, and every term in its second line has weight zero. The only coordinate pairs that could have weight -1 are a kernel input and a quotient output; their coefficients are zero. The weight degeneration of Remark 2.16 therefore discards exactly the terms involving \(\eta_{r,i}(f)\).

The remaining quotient-to-quotient coefficients _c_<sub>_r-i_</sub> express multiplication from _V<sub>b</sub>_ to _V_<sub>_S+b_</sub>. The remaining kernel-to-kernel coefficients _c_<sub>_r-j_</sub> express multiplication from _V_<sub>_b_-2</sub> to _V_<sub>_S+b_-2</sub>. Taking their dependence on the separate shared inputs into account identifies the two retained coefficient tensors as

\(C_+=\mathcal{C}_n(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},b+1),C_-=\mathcal{C}_n(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},b-1).\)

They share the first _n_-2 legs and occupy disjoint matched sectors in the last two legs. Their last-input dimensions are _b_+1 and _b_-1, and their output dimensions are _S+b_+1 and _S+b_-1, respectively. These dimensions agree with Definition 4.1.

Write _C_=C_<sub>n</sub>(a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-2</sub>_,b_). For every \(\pi\in S_n\) and every real number \(0\le\theta\le 1\), degeneration monotonicity and Corollary 3.2 imply

\(2^{p_{n-1,n}^{(\phi\pi)}}\phi_\pi(C)\ge exp\big(p_{n-1,n}^{(\phi\pi)}H(\theta,1-\theta)\big)\phi_\pi(C_+)^\theta\phi_\pi(C_-)^{1-\theta}.\)

The factor on the left is the spectral value of the additional edge tensor \(E_{n-1,n}^{(2)}\). The entropy factor on the right uses the same pair of legs, because these are precisely the two unshared legs of the retained blocks.

Use one common value of \(\theta\) for all permutations. Multiply over all \(\pi\in S_n\), take the power \(1/(n!t_\phi)\), and apply (2). By the definition of \(P_\phi\), the resulting inequality is<tbc>

\(2P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},b)\ge e^{H(\theta,1-\theta)}P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},b+1)^\theta P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},b-1)^{1-\theta}.\)

<tbc>Put \(A=P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},b+1)\) and \(B=P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},b-1)\). Both are positive by Lemma 4.6, so we may choose \(\theta=A/(A+B)\). Then \(A/\theta=B/(1-\theta)=A+B\), and<tbc>

\(e^{H(\theta,1-\theta)}A^\theta B^{1-\theta}=\big(\frac{A}{\theta}\big)^\theta\big(\frac{B}{1-\theta}\big)^{1-\theta}=A+B.\)

Substituting this identity proves the claimed concavity inequality.

## 4.3 Shifted tripling

We next compare an input length _h_ with 3_h+S_, where _S_ is the sum of the other input degrees. The resulting factor of three provides a lower bound on a long increment of the profile; concavity will then give a lower bound on a single increment. The construction extends \[Ope26a, Lemma 4.2\]. We specify its coordinate sectors by their offsets and lengths, using the same convention as Theorem 3.1.

**Lemma 4.9** (shifted tripling)**.** _Let_ \(n\ge 3\) _be an integer, let_ \(\phi\in\Phi_n\)_, and let_ \(P_\phi\) _be its profile. For all positive integers a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-2</sub>_,h, put_ \(S=\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}(a_j-1)\)_. Then_

\(P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},3h+S)\ge 3P_\phi(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},h).\)

_Proof._ Set _B_=3_h+S_. Index a supported entry of C_<sub>n</sub>(a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-2</sub>_,B_) by its shared input indices _i_<sub>1</sub>_,...,i_<sub>_n_-2</sub>, its last-input index _y_, and its output index _z_. The defining conditions are<tbc>

\(0\le i_j<a_j(1\le j\le n-2),0\le y<B,z=y+\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}i_j.\)

<tbc>In particular, \(0\le\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}i_j\le S\) and \(0\le z<B+S\). Introduce three last-input lengths _b_<sub>0</sub>=_b_<sub>2</sub>=_h_ and _b_<sub>1</sub>=_h+S_, and three output lengths _c_<sub>0</sub>=_c_<sub>2</sub>=_h+S_ and _c_<sub>1</sub>=_h_. For \(r\in\{0,1,2\}\), put

\(\beta_r=\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}b_t,\gamma_r=\sum_{t=0}^{r-1}c_t,Y_r=\{\beta_r+i:0\le i<b_r\},Z_r=\{\gamma_r+j:0\le j<c_r\}.\)

The sums for _r_=0 are empty. These are disjoint partitions of \[_B_\]<sub>0</sub> and \[_B+S_\]<sub>0</sub>, since \(\sum_{r=0}^2b_r=B\) and \(\sum_{r=0}^2c_r=B+S\). Their offsets satisfy \(\beta_0=\gamma_0=0\), \(\beta_1=h\), \(\gamma_1=h+S\), and \(\beta_2=\gamma_2=2h+S\).

Give a last-input coordinate weight +1 when it belongs to _Y_<sub>1</sub>, and weight zero otherwise. Give an output coordinate weight -1 when it belongs to _Z_<sub>1</sub>, and weight zero otherwise. All shared coordinates have weight zero. If \(y\in Y_0\), then _y\<h_ and \(z\le h-1+S\), so \(z\in Z_0\). If \(y\in Y_2\), then \(2h+S\le y<B\) and \(2h+S\le z<B+S\), so \(z\in Z_2\). Consequently, \(z\in Z_1\) requires \(y\in Y_1\).

It follows that every supported entry has nonnegative total weight. The entries with \(y\in Y_r\) and \(z\in Z_r\), for some \(r\in\{0,1,2\}\), have weight zero. Every other supported entry has \(y\in Y_1\) and \(z\in Z_0\cup Z_2\), and hence has weight +1. Applying the weight degeneration retains exactly the three matched blocks in the sectors \(Y_r\times Z_r\).

Let _C_=C_<sub>n</sub>(a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-2</sub>_,h_). In sector _r_=0, write \(y=y'\) and \(z=z'\). In sector _r_=2, write \(y=2h+S+y'\) and \(z=2h+S+z'\). In either case, the support condition becomes

\(0\le y'<h,0\le z'<h+S,z'=y'+\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}i_j.\)

Every choice of the shared input indices and \(y'\in[h]_0\) gives exactly one allowed \(z'\). Thus, after these translations of the last two coordinates, each outer block equals _C_ in the original shared coordinates.

To identify the middle block, define<tbc>

\(\bar{i}_j=a_j-1-i_j(1\le j\le n-2),r=z-(h+S).\)

<tbc>The middle output interval gives \(0\le r<h\). Replacing _i<sub>j</sub>_ by \(a_j-1-\bar{i}_j\) in the support equation gives

\(y=h+r+\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}\bar{i}_j,z=h+S+r.\)

Conversely, choose arbitrary integers \(0\le\bar{i}_j<a_j\) for \(1\le j\le n-2\) and \(0\le r<h\). These equations give \(h\le y\le 2h+S-1\) and \(h+S\le z\le 2h+S-1\), so they specify a supported entry in the middle block. Therefore the displayed parametrization describes all and only its supported entries, each with coefficient one.

Reflect each shared input basis, and subtract _h_ and _h+S_ from the last-input and output indices, respectively. With \(y'=y-h\), the equation is \(y'=r+\sum_{j=1}^{n-2}\bar{i}_j\). This is the defining support equation of _C_ with its last two legs exchanged: _r_ is its length-_h_ input, while \(y'\) is its length-(_h+S_) output. Let \(\sigma\in S_n\) denote that exchange. The middle block is thus locally isomorphic to \(\sigma C\). This identification concerns the middle block as an individual tensor; it does not apply a block-dependent map to the shared legs of the whole three-block tensor.

Apply Corollary 3.2 to the retained blocks with probability vector (1/3,1/3,1/3), whose entropy is ln3. For every \(\pi\in S_n\), degeneration monotonicity gives<tbc>

\(\phi_\pi\big(\mathcal{C}_n(a_1,\dots,a_{n-2},B)\big)\ge 3^{p_{n-1,n}^{(\phi_\pi)}}\phi_\pi(C)^{2/3}\phi_\pi(\sigma C)^{1/3}.\)

<tbc>Since \(\pi\mapsto\pi\sigma\) is a bijection of _S<sub>n</sub>_,<tbc>

\(\prod_{\pi\in S_n}\phi_\pi(\sigma C)=\prod_{\pi\in S_n}\phi_\pi(C).\)

<tbc>Multiplying the spectral inequalities over all \(\pi\in S_n\), and then taking the power \(1/(n!t_\phi)\), therefore gives

## 4.4 Diagonal growth

We now extend the diagonal-growth step of OpenAI \[Ope26a, Section 5 and Lemma 5.1\] to _n_-1 input coordinates. Discrete concavity bounds a long increment by its first step, while shifted tripling gives a lower bound on that long increment. We apply the resulting estimate along a path that increases each coordinate once. Keeping track of all _n_-1 steps gives the exponent 2(_n_-1)_/n_. Comparing this growth with the linear rank bound from Subsection 4.1 then bounds the average spectral edge weight.

**Lemma 4.10** (diagonal growth)**.** _Let_ \(n\ge 3\) _be an integer. Suppose that_ \(F:\mathbb{N}_{>0}^{n-1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) _is symmetric, that F_(1_,...,_1)=1_, and that it satisfies the concavity and shifted tripling inequalities in Lemmas 4.8 and 4.9, with F in place of_ \(P_\phi\)_. Then, for every positive integer a,_<tbc>

\(F(\underbrace{a,\dots,a}_{n-1})\ge a^{2(n-1)/n}.\)

_Proof._ For every positive integer _a_, write _Da=F(a,...,a_). We first compare _D__a_+1 with _Da_. Start from (_a,...,a_) and increase its coordinates one at a time until reaching (_a_+1_,...,a_+1). Fix an integer _j_ with \(1\le j\le n-1\), and consider the step that increases coordinate _j_. The earlier coordinates already equal _a_+1, and the later coordinates still equal _a_. Define \(F_j(b)=\underbrace{F(a+1,\dots,a+1,b,\underbrace{a,\dots,a}_{j-1})}_{n-1-j\text{coordinates}})(b\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}).\) The total degree in the other coordinates is \(S_j=\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}a+\sum_{i=j+1}^{n-1}(a-1)=(j-1)a+(n-1-j)(a-1)\le(n-2)a.\) By shifted tripling, \(F_j(3a+S_j)\ge 3F_j(a)\). Concavity gives \(F_j(h+1)-F_j(h)\le F_j(h)-F_j(h-1)\) for every integer \(h\ge 2\). Thus every forward difference starting at an integer \(h\ge a\) is at most _Fj(a_+1)-_Fj(a_). In particular, \(2F_j(a)\le F_j(3a+S_j)-F_j(a)\)
\(=\sum_{h=a}^{3a+S_j-1}\big(F_j(h+1)-F_j(h)\big)\)
\(\le(2a+S_j)\big(F_j(a+1)-F_j(a)\big).\) Since \(2a+S_j\le na\) and _Fj(a)\>_0, division by 2_a+Sj_ gives \(F_j(a+1)\ge\left(1+\frac{2}{2a+S_j}\right)F_j(a)\ge\left(1+\frac{2}{na}\right)F_j(a).\) The values at successive steps agree: _F_1(_a_)=_Da_, _Fj(a_+1)=_F__j_+1(_a_) for \(1\le j_n_-1(_a_+1)=_D__a_+1. Multiplying the _n_-1 inequalities therefore gives \(D_{a+1}\ge\left(1+\frac{2}{na}\right)^{n-1}D_a.\) (4) This argument also applies when _a_=1, since concavity at input length 2 compares the first two forward differences. For every positive real number _x_ and every real \(r\ge 1\), Bernoulli’s inequality gives \((1+x)^r\ge 1+rx\). With _x_=2/(_na_) and _r=n/_2, it follows that \(\left(1+\frac{2}{na}\right)^{n/2}\ge 1+\frac{1}{a}.\) Raise this inequality to the positive power 2(_n_-1)_/n_ and combine it with (4). We find \(\frac{D_{a+1}}{D_a}\ge\left(\frac{a+1}{a}\right)^{2(n-1)/n}.\) Finally, _D_1=1. Multiplying the last inequality for _a_=1_,...,A_-1 gives \(D_A\ge\prod_{a=1}^{A-1}\left(\frac{a+1}{a}\right)^{2(n-1)/n}=A^{2(n-1)/n}\) for every integer \(A\ge 2\). ## 4.5 The complete graph bound and its consequences

We apply the preceding growth estimate to the symmetric spectral profile \(P_\phi\). Its lower growth rate, compared with the interpolation upper bound from Subsection 4.1, constrains the average edge weight \(t_\phi\). Since a complete graph contains every pair of vertices as an edge, this average determines its value under \(\phi\). Spectral duality then gives the desired rank upper bound, while a maximum cut gives the lower bound.

**Theorem 4.11** (complete graph bound)**.** _For every integer_ \(n\ge 2\)_, over the complex numbers,_

\(\left\lfloor\frac{n^2}{4}\right\rfloor\le\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\text{R}}\big(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n)\big)\le\frac{n^2}{4}.\)

_Proof._ First suppose that \(n\ge 3\), and fix an arbitrary spectral point \(\phi\in\Phi_n\). Let \(P_\phi\) and \(t_\phi\) be as in Definition 4.5. Lemma 4.6 gives positivity, symmetry, and \(P_\phi(1,\dots,1)=1\). Lemmas 4.8 and 4.9 give the two inequalities required by Lemma 4.10. Therefore, for every positive integer _a_,<tbc>

\(a^{2(n-1)/n}\le P_\phi(a,\dots,a)\le\big((n-1)(a-1)+1\big)^{1/t_\phi}.\)

<tbc>For \(a\ge 2\), take logarithms and divide by log_a_. The expression ((_n_-1)(_a_-1)+1)_/a_ tends to the positive constant _n_-1. Hence<tbc>

\(\frac{2(n-1)}{n}\le\frac{1}{t_\phi}\frac{\mathrm{log}((n-1)(a-1)+1)}{\mathrm{log}a}\longrightarrow\frac{1}{t_\phi}.\)

<tbc>It follows that \(t_\phi\le n/(2(n-1))\). By the definition of the average spectral edge weight \(t_\phi\) and Lemma 4.4,

\(\phi(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n))=2\sum_{1\le i<j\le n}p_{i,j}^{(\phi)}=2^{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}t_\phi}\le 2^{n^2/4}.\)

This holds for every \(\phi\in\Phi_n\). Taking the maximum over \(\Phi_n\) and applying Theorem 2.19 gives \(\widetilde{\text{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n))\le 2^{n^2/4}\). The argument fixes _n_ throughout; only the input length _a_ tends to infinity in the preceding comparison.

For the lower bound, Proposition A.4 gives \(\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\text{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n))\ge\mathrm{MaxCut}(K_n)\). A cut with _s_ vertices on one side has _s(n-s_) crossing edges, where \(1\le s\le n-1\). Since _s(n-s_)=_n_<sup>2</sup>/4-(_s-n/_2)<sup>2</sup>, its maximum is attained at \(s=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) or \(s=\lceil n/2\rceil\), and equals \(\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor\). This proves both inequalities for \(n\ge 3\).

Finally, GT<sub>2</sub>(_K_<sub>2</sub>) is the \(2\times 2\) identity matrix viewed as a complex second-order tensor. Its _N_-th Kronecker power has matrix rank 2_<sup>N</sup>_, so its asymptotic rank is 2. Thus both bounds are equal to 1 when _n_=2, completing the proof.

The next two consequences identify the questions from \[CVZ19\] answered by the theorem. The edge exponent \(\tau(G)\) is defined in Definition 2.22.

**Corollary 4.12** (maximum-cut equality for even complete graphs)**.** _For every positive integer m,_

\(\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\text{R}}\big(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_{2m})\big)=\mathrm{MaxCut}(K_{2m})=m^2,\tau(K_{2m})=\frac{m}{2m-1}.\)

_Thus the equality asked for in \[CVZ19, Question 1.3.2\] holds for every even complete graph._

_Proof._ Apply Theorem 4.11 with _n_=2_m_. Its lower and upper bounds both equal _m_<sup>2</sup>. A balanced cut of _K_<sub>2_m_</sub> has _m_<sup>2</sup> edges and is a maximum cut. Finally, _K_<sub>2_m_</sub> has \((\genfrac(){pt}{2}{2m}{2}=m(2m-1)\) edges, so dividing the exponent _m_<sup>2</sup> by this number gives the formula for \(\tau(K_{2m})\).

**Corollary 4.13** (edge exponents below two thirds)**.** _For every integer_ \(n\ge 5\),

\(\tau(K_n)\le\frac{n}{2(n-1)}<\frac{2}{3}.\)

_In particular, the existence question in \[CVZ19, Question 1.3.1\] has an affirmative answer for every_ \(n\ge 5\)_. Moreover,_ \(lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\tau(K_n)=1/2\).

_Proof._ Divide the upper bound in Theorem 4.11 by |_E(K<sub>n</sub>_)|=_n(n_-1)/2. The strict inequality _n/_(2(_n_-1))_\<_2/3 is equivalent to 3_n\<_4_n_-4, or _n\>_4. For the limit, both bounds in the theorem give

\(\frac{\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor}{\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}}\le\tau(K_n)\le\frac{n}{2(n-1)}.\)

The two bounding quantities tend to 1/2, which proves the claim.

For odd _n_, the upper bound still exceeds the maximum-cut lower bound by 1/4. Section 5 studies whether further combinations of the polynomial constructions can close this gap. It specifies the allowed operations and constructs a numerical certificate that limits every derivation in that system.

## 5 An Operational Barrier for the Polynomial Method

The polynomial constructions in Section 4 give the complete-graph upper bound _n_<sup>2</sup>/4 in Subsection 4.5. We now examine whether their further combinations can improve this threshold. Amanov, van den Berg, and Zuiddam \[ABZ26, Section 5\] proved that the three-leg polynomial ingredients cannot yield a matrix multiplication exponent below 9/4, even when the ingredients are combined repeatedly. We extend their symmetric certificate to _n_ legs. Its threshold is _n_<sup>2</sup>/4, and its growth on polynomial tensors matches the diagonal exponent in Subsection 4.4.

The proof separates the tensor constructions from their numerical analysis. We first define formal expressions and a resource form of simultaneous separation. We then specify the permitted derivations and verify that each rule describes a valid tensor degeneration. A comparison function supplies the numerical inequalities needed by these rules; extending it to expressions gives the barrier. The certificate is monotone for this explicitly generated relation on expressions. It is not asserted to be a spectral point on Tens_<sub>n</sub>_(C). Throughout this section, \(n\ge 3\) is an integer. We allow arbitrary positive integer edge dimensions in the auxiliary expressions, but state the final barrier for GT<sub>2</sub>(_K<sub>n</sub>_), in the same normalization as Theorem 1.1.

### 5.1 Formal expressions and polynomial resources

A formal expression records how a tensor is built, including which coordinates are shared in a partial direct sum. We begin with polynomial atoms whose support treats every leg symmetrically. This convention will allow the tripling rule to retain the original shared coordinates in all three output blocks.

**Definition 5.1** (polynomial atoms)**.** A vector **x**=(_x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>n</sub>_) of positive integers is _admissible_ if, with \(M=max_{1\le i\le n}x_i\),<tbc>

\(\sum_{i=1}^nx_i=2M+n-2.\)

\(\mathrm{ev}(\mathsf{C}_\mathbf{x})=\sum_{0\le u_i<x_i\left(1\le i\le n\right)\sum_{i=1}^nu_i=M-1}\otimes_{i=1}^ne_{u_i}^{(x_i)}.\)

\(D=1+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}(a_i-1),\mathsf{C}_n(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1})=\mathsf{C}_{(a_1,\dots,a_{n-1},D)}.\)

Reversing the last coordinate identifies ev(C_<sub>n</sub>(a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-1</sub>)) with C_<sub>n</sub>(a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a_<sub>_n_-1</sub>). Extend ev recursively by evaluating \(\oplus_K\) and \(\otimes_K\) with the coordinate conventions in Definition 2.2, and by evaluating \(X\boxplus_eY\) on the already specified coordinate representatives using Definition 2.9. Thus the two sectors are disjoint and matched on legs _u,v_, and their coordinates on every other leg are shared. A permutation \(\pi\in S_n\) (Definition 2.11) acts on expressions by permuting the entries of every atom, distributing over the two full operations, and mapping \(X\boxplus_eY\) to \((\pi X)\boxplus_{\pi e}(\pi Y)\). \(\mathbf{E}_{i,j}^{(q)}=\mathsf{C}_\mathbf{x},x_s=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
q, & s\in\{i,j\}, \\
1, & s\notin\{i,j\},

Their evaluations are \(E_{i,j}^{(q)}\), I_<sub>n</sub>(R_), and GT_<sub>q</sub>(K<sub>n</sub>_), respectively. We first prove a form of separation that retains the auxiliary polynomial tensor. For three legs this is the resource form in \[ABZ26, Proposition 3.5\]. The same square-weight argument<tbc>

can enforce all shared labels simultaneously, with the number of blocks and the dimension of the retained edge chosen independently.

**Lemma 5.4** (separation with a polynomial resource)**.** _Let_ \(m,t\ge 1\) _be integers, and let_ \(X_0,\dots,X_{m-1}\in\mathcal{F}_n\) _have equal dimensions on their first n_-2 _legs. Put e_=(_n_-1_,n_) _and_ \(A=X_0\boxplus_e\cdots\boxplus_eX_{m-1}\)_. Then_<tbc>

## A Flattening Rank, Cut Bounds, and Triangle Covers

We give the rank bounds used in the introduction. The flattening argument and its graph-cut specialization are standard; see Christandl, Vrana, and Zuiddam \[CVZ19, Definition 1.1.19, Proposition 1.1.20, and Example 1.1.21\]. We state them in our coordinate conventions, include the bipartite equality case, and then give the triangle-cover argument with OpenAI’s improved matrix multiplication bound. Appendix B treats asymptotic subrank separately.

**Definition A.1** (flattening rank)**.** Let \(k\ge 2\) be an integer, let _T_ be a complex _k_-th order tensor, and choose coordinates of positive dimensions (_d_<sub>1</sub>_,...,d<sub>k</sub>_) for _T_. If _T_=0, use the zero coefficient table of these dimensions. Let \(\varnothing\neq S\unknown\{1,\dots,k\}\) and write <o>_S_</o>={1_,...,k_}\\_S_. In these coordinates, the _flattening across S_ is the matrix Flat_<sub>S</sub>(T_) with rows indexed by \(\mathbf{a}\in\prod_{v\in S}[d_v]_0\) and columns indexed by \(\mathbf{b}\in\prod_{v\in\overline{S}}[d_v]_0\), defined by

\(\mathrm{Flat}_S(T)_{\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}}=T_{c_1,\dots,c_k},c_v=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
a_v, & v\in S, \\
b_v, & v\in\overline{S},
\end{array}\right.(1\le v\le k).\)

The indices on each side are ordered by increasing vertex label and then lexicographically. The _flattening rank_ is FR_<sub>S</sub>(T_)=rank(Flat_<sub>S</sub>(T_)). A different representative of a nonzero tensor permutes the rows and columns, so this rank is independent of the representative. For _T_=0, every choice gives a zero matrix, and hence FR_<sub>S</sub>_(0)=0.

**Lemma A.2** (properties of flattening rank)**.** _Let_ \(k\ge 2\) _be an integer, let A,B be complex k-th order tensors, and let_ \(\varnothing\neq S\unknown\{1,\dots,k\}\)_, with complement <o>S</o>. Then_

\(\mathrm{Q}(A)\le\mathrm{FR}_S(A)\le\mathrm{R}(A),\mathrm{FR}_S(A\otimes_KB)=\mathrm{FR}_S(A)\mathrm{FR}_S(B).\)

_Moreover,_ \(A\unknown B\) _implies_ \(\mathrm{FR}_S(A)\le\mathrm{FR}_S(B)\)_, and_ FR_<sub>S</sub>_(l_<sub>k</sub>(q_))=_q for every nonnegative integer q._

_Proof._ The claims involving a zero tensor follow from R(0)=Q(0)=FR_<sub>S</sub>_(0)=0 and the fact that \(A\unknown 0\) implies _A_=0. We may therefore assume that _A_ and _B_ are nonzero and work in fixed coordinates.

A simple tensor \(x_1\otimes_C\cdots\otimes_Cx_k\) flattens to the outer product of the vector \(\otimes_{K_{v\in S}}x_v\) and the vector \(\otimes_{K_{v\in\overline{S}}}x_v\). It therefore has matrix rank at most 1. A rank decomposition of _A_ into _r_ simple tensors gives a sum of _r_ matrices of rank at most 1, proving \(\mathrm{FR}_S(A)\le\mathrm{R}(A)\).

Suppose that local matrices _L_<sub>1</sub>_,...,L<sub>k</sub>_ map _B_ to _A_. Expanding the entries in Definition 2.4 gives

\(\mathrm{Flat}_S(A)=\left(\otimes_{K_{v\in\overline{S}}}L_v\right)\mathrm{Flat}_S(B)\left(\otimes_{K_{v\in\overline{S}}}L_v\right)^\mathsf{T}.\)

Here the products are the usual Kronecker products of matrices, with their factors in increasing vertex order. Multiplication on the left or right cannot increase matrix rank, so \(\mathrm{FR}_S(A)\le\mathrm{FR}_S(B)\). For \(q\ge 1\), the flattening of l_<sub>k</sub>(q_) has exactly one entry 1 in each position whose row and column are constant tuples with the same value in \[_q_\]<sub>0</sub>. These positions use _q_ distinct rows and _q_ distinct columns; all other entries are zero. Its rank is therefore _q_. The assertion for _q_=0 follows from the definition of l_<sub>k</sub>_(0). Applying monotonicity to \(\mathrm{l}_k(\mathrm{Q}(A))\unknown A\) proves \(\mathrm{Q}(A)\le\mathrm{FR}_S(A)\).

After separate permutations of its rows and columns, \(\mathrm{Flat}_S(A\otimes_KB)\) is the matrix Kronecker product of Flat_<sub>S</sub>(A_) and Flat_<sub>S</sub>(B_). To recall why matrix rank is multiplicative under this<tbc>

operation, invertible row and column operations put a matrix of rank _r_ into a rectangular matrix with an \(r\times r\) identity block and zeros elsewhere. Applying the Kronecker products of these operations to two matrices of ranks _r_ and _s_ produces a matrix with exactly _rs_ independent nonzero rows and columns. Its rank is _rs_, proving the remaining identity.

The following calculation identifies the flattenings used in the cut bounds of \[CVZ19, Example 1.1.21\].
