\(\mathrm{FR}_S(E_{u,v}^{(q)})=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
q, & (u,v)\in\delta_G(S), \\
1, & (u,v)\notin\delta_G(S).
\end{array}\right.\)

_If G is bipartite, then_ \(\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_q(G))=|E(G)|\mathrm{log}_2q=\mathrm{MaxCut}(G)\mathrm{log}_2q\)_. In particular, the lower bound gives_ \(\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n))\ge|n^2/4|\) _for every integer_ \(n\ge 2\).

_Proof._ Fix a nonempty proper subset \(S\subset V(G)\). Lemmas A.2 and A.3 give, for every positive integer _N_,

\(\mathrm{R}(\mathsf{GT}_q(G)^{\otimes K}N)\ge\mathrm{FR}_S(\mathsf{GT}_q(G)^{\otimes K}N)=\mathrm{FR}_S(\mathsf{GT}_q(G))^N=q^{N|\delta_G(S)|}.\)

Taking _N_-th roots, letting \(N\rightarrow\infty\), and taking base-two logarithms gives \(\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_q(G))\ge|\delta_G(S)|\mathrm{log}_2q\). Since \(q\ge 2\), we have log<sub>2</sub>_q\>_0, so maximizing over _S_ gives the first assertion.

Suppose that _G_ is bipartite and has at least one edge. Its bipartition is a cut crossed by every edge, so MaxCut(_G_)=|_E(G_)|. The defining expansion of GT_<sub>q</sub>(G_) has one simple tensor for each of the _q_<sup>|_E(G_)|</sup> edge labelings. Hence \(\mathrm{R}(\mathsf{GT}_q(G))\le q^{|E(G)|}\), and taking Kronecker powers<tbc>

of this decomposition gives \(\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_q(G))\le q^{|E(G)|}\). Taking base-two logarithms and combining with the lower bound proves the claimed equality. If _G_ has no edges, then GT_<sub>q</sub>(G_)=l_<sub>k</sub>_(1) for _k_=|_V(G_)|, so the same equality holds with all three quantities equal to zero.

A cut of _K<sub>n</sub>_ with _s_ vertices on one side has _s(n-s_) crossing edges. Since _s(n-s_)=_n_<sup>2</sup>/4-(_s-n/_2)<sup>2</sup>, its maximum over integers \(1\le s\le n-1\) is \(\lfloor n^2/4\rfloor\).

We next state the triangle version of the covering argument in \[CVZ19, Proposition 1.1.25\], allowing a graph to be covered with unequal multiplicities. A triangle cover may use the same triangle more than once. The symbolic bound in terms of \(\omega\) is the covering argument; the numerical value 3/4 per edge specifically uses \(\omega\le 9/4\) from OpenAI \[Ope26a\].

**Theorem A.5** (triangle-cover upper bound)**.** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be a finite simple undirected graph with_ \(|V|\ge 3\) _and_ \(E\neq\varnothing\)_. Let M,r be positive integers, and let_ \(\Delta_1,\dots,\Delta_M\) _be triangles of G such that every edge of G belongs to at least r of them, counting repetitions. Then_<tbc>

\(log_2\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_2(G))\le\frac{M\omega}{r}.\)

<tbc>_In particular, for every integer_ \(n\ge 3\),

\(log_2\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_n))\le\frac{\omega}{3}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}\le\frac{3}{4}\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2},\tau(K_n)\le\frac{3}{4}.\)

_The last inequalities use OpenAI’s bound_ \(\omega\le 9/4\) _\[Ope26a\]._

_Proof._ Write _k_=|_V_| and label _V_ by {1_,...,k_}. For each \(1\le h\le M\), let _T<sub>h</sub>_ be the _k_-th order graph tensor supported on the three edges of \(\Delta_h\), with dimension 1 at every vertex outside that triangle. Appending legs of dimension 1 does not change rank: a decomposition extends by appending the scalar 1 on those legs, and conversely contracting those legs removes them from any decomposition. The same observation applies to every Kronecker power. Hence \(\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(T_h)=\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_2(K_3))=2^\omega\) for \(1\le h\le M\).

For every edge \(e\in E\), let \(r_e=|\{h|1\le h\le M,e\in E(\Delta_h)\}|\). Rearranging the edge factors in \(B=\otimes_{Kh=1}^MT_h\) gives _r<sub>e</sub>_ copies of the edge tensor on _e_. For each _e_, choose the same _r_ occurrences to retain at both endpoints. Project the coordinates in the other _r<sub>e</sub>-r_ occurrences onto the coordinate with label 0 at both endpoints. Each removed copy then contributes the scalar 1, and exactly _r_ copies remain on every edge. These projections act separately at each vertex and give \(\mathsf{GT}_2(G)^{\otimes_Kr}\unknown B\). Asymptotic rank is monotone under restriction and submultiplicative under Kronecker product. Both facts follow by taking ordinary rank inequalities for the _N_-th powers, then _N_-th roots and limits. Also, its definition gives \(\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(T^{\otimes_Kr})=\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(T)^r\), by taking the subsequence of powers divisible by _r_. Therefore

\(\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(\mathsf{GT}_2(G))^r\le\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(B)\le\prod_{h=1}^M\widetilde{\mathsf{R}}(T_h)=2^{M\omega}.\)

Taking base-2 logarithms and dividing by _r_ proves the general bound.

For _K<sub>n</sub>_, use every triangle once. There are \(M=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{3}\) triangles, and an edge belongs to exactly _r=n_-2 of them, one for each choice of a third vertex. Thus \(M/r=\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}/3\). Substituting \(\omega\le 9/4\) and dividing by \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{n}{2}\) gives the stated bounds.

## B Asymptotic Subrank and the Minimum Cut

We give a tensor-language proof of the minimum-cut formula of Vrana and Christandl \[VC17, Theorem 1\]. Their theorem concerns hypergraphs and is stated in terms of entanglement conversion. For graphs, we retain their orthogonal-representation construction, give the local maps explicitly, and verify the passage from degeneration to ordinary asymptotic subrank. The aim is to select many edge labelings such that the labels at any one vertex determine the entire labeling. The following definition and lemma give the required linear equations.

**Definition B.1** (general-position orthogonal representation)**.** Let _H_ be a finite simple graph with vertex set _W_, and let _d_ be a positive integer with \(d\le|W|\). A _general-position orthogonal representation_ of _H_ in R_<sup>d</sup>_ is a family \((c_w)_{w\in W}\) of vectors in R_<sup>d</sup>_ such that \(\langle c_u,c_v\rangle=0\) for every two distinct nonadjacent vertices \(u,v\in W\), and every subfamily of at most _d_ vectors is linearly independent. Here \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^dx_jy_j\).

The _line graph L(G_) of a graph _G_ has vertex set _E(G_); two distinct vertices of _L(G_) are adjacent exactly when the corresponding edges of _G_ share an endpoint.

The next lemma is the graph case of \[VC17, Theorem 3\]. Its real-vector input is the theorem of Lovász, Saks, and Schrijver \[LSS89, Theorem 1.1\], with the corrected proof in \[LSS00, Theorem 1\]. We include the rational approximation argument to obtain the integer weights used below.

**Lemma B.2** (integral orthogonal representations)**.** _Let G be a finite connected simple graph with at least three vertices. Put m_=|_E(G_)|, \(\ell=\mathrm{MinCut}(G)\)_, and_ \(d=m-\ell\)_. Then_ \(d\ge 1\)_, and L(G_) _has a general-position orthogonal representation_ \((c_e)_{e\in E(G)}\) _with_ \(c_e\in\mathbb{Z}^d\) _for every_ \(e\in E(G)\).

_Proof._ If _G_ has \(k\ge 3\) vertices, then \(\ell\le\mathrm{min}_{v\in V(G)}\mathrm{deg}(v)\le 2m/k<m\). Also \(\ell\ge 1\) because _G_ is connected. Consequently \(1\le d\le m-1\).

Deleting fewer than \(\ell\) edges leaves _G_ connected: otherwise a component of the remaining graph would give a cut of _G_ with fewer than \(\ell\) edges. It follows that deleting fewer than \(\ell\) vertices leaves _L(G_) connected. Indeed, the remaining vertices are the edges of the connected remaining graph, and a path in that graph connects any two of its edges by a sequence of incident edges. Thus _L(G_) is \(\ell\)-vertex-connected: it has more than \(\ell\) vertices and remains connected after deleting any set of fewer than \(\ell\) vertices.

The theorem of Lovász, Saks, and Schrijver \[LSS89, LSS00\] states that an (_m-d_)-vertex- connected graph on _m_ vertices admits a general-position orthogonal representation in R_<sup>d</sup>_. Apply it to _L(G_) and fix such a representation _a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>m</sub>_, after ordering its vertices by the edges of _G_.

We now obtain rational vectors while preserving all orthogonality constraints. For each \(1\le i\le m\), let _A<sub>i</sub>_ be the set of indices _j\<i_ whose vertices are not adjacent to vertex _i_ in _L(G_). Every vertex of an \(\ell\)-vertex-connected graph has degree at least \(\ell\): otherwise deleting its fewer than \(\ell\) neighbors would isolate it while leaving another vertex. Hence \(|A_i|\le m-1-\ell=d-1\). Given vectors _f_<sub>1</sub>_,...,f<sub>m</sub>_ sufficiently close to _a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>m</sub>_, define vectors _z_<sub>1</sub>_,...,z<sub>m</sub>_ in order. Let _B<sub>i</sub>_ be the matrix whose columns are _z<sub>j</sub>_ for \(j\in A_i\), ordered increasingly, and set

\(z_i=f_i-B_i(B_i^\mathsf{T}B_i)^{-1}B_i^\mathsf{T}f_i.\)

If _A<sub>i</sub>_ is empty, the subtracted term is defined to be zero. At _f<sub>i</sub>=a<sub>i</sub>_ for every _i_, induction gives _z<sub>i</sub>=a<sub>i</sub>_: the columns of _B<sub>i</sub>_ are independent by general position, and _a<sub>i</sub>_ is orthogonal to all of them. Thus every nonempty Gram matrix \(B_i^\mathsf{T}B_i\) is invertible at this choice.

There are only finitely many such matrices. Induction on _i_ and continuity of matrix inversion therefore give an open neighborhood of (_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>m</sub>_) in which every displayed inverse exists and every _z<sub>i</sub>_ depends continuously on (_f_<sub>1</sub>_,...,f<sub>m</sub>_). Shrinking this neighborhood if necessary keeps every \(d\times d\) determinant formed from distinct vectors _z<sub>i</sub>_ nonzero, since there are finitely many and all are nonzero at (_a_<sub>1</sub>_,...,a<sub>m</sub>_). The resulting vectors are in general position. Moreover, _z<sub>i</sub>_ is orthogonal to each column of _B<sub>i</sub>_, so every required orthogonality relation holds exactly.

Choose all coordinates of _f_<sub>1</sub>_,...,f<sub>m</sub>_ rational within this open neighborhood. The displayed formula then produces rational coordinates for every _z<sub>i</sub>_, because it uses only rational matrix operations and inverses of invertible rational matrices. Multiply all vectors by a common positive integer that clears their denominators. This preserves orthogonality and linear independence and gives the required integral vectors _c<sub>e</sub>_.

We also use an elementary exact restriction to absorb the interpolation overhead. It extends the one-copy extraction for paths discussed in \[VC17, Section 3\] to any connected graph by selecting a spanning tree.

**Lemma B.3** (a diagonal restriction from a spanning tree)**.** _For every finite connected simple graph G on_ \(k\ge 2\) _vertices and every integer_ \(q\ge 2\)_, we have_ \(\mathsf{I}_k(q)\unknown\mathsf{GT}_q(G)\).

_Proof._ Choose a spanning tree _F_ of _G_. Every vertex is incident to at least one edge of _F_. At vertex _v_, consider the basis vector indexed by the labels on the edges incident to _v_. Send this basis vector to \(e_a^{(q)}\) if all incident edges outside _F_ have label 0 and all incident edges in _F_ have the same label \(a\in[q]_0\). Send it to zero otherwise. This specifies a linear map on every leg.

A surviving global edge labeling has label 0 on every edge outside _F_. If _a<sub>v</sub>_ is the common tree- edge label at vertex _v_, then a tree edge (_u,v_) has both labels _a<sub>u</sub>_ and _a<sub>v</sub>_, so _a<sub>u</sub>=a<sub>v</sub>_. Connectivity of _F_ forces _a<sub>v</sub>=a_ for all vertices and a single \(a\in[q]_0\). Conversely, each such _a_ gives exactly one surviving labeling. The image of the graph tensor is therefore \(\sum_{a=0}^{q-1}e_a^{(q)}\otimes_C\cdots\otimes_Ce_a^{(q)}=\mathsf{I}_k(q)\).

We now combine these two ingredients. The orthogonal representation will select a large set of edge labelings that are distinguishable at every vertex. The spanning-tree restriction will then absorb the interpolation overhead, allowing us to pass from a degeneration to ordinary asymptotic subrank.

**Theorem B.4** (Vrana-Christandl \[VC17\])**.** _For every finite simple undirected graph G with at least two vertices,_<tbc>

\(\mathrm{log}_2\widetilde{\mathsf{Q}}(\mathsf{GT}_2(G))=\mathrm{MinCut}(G).\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Let _V(G_)={1_,...,k_} and put \(\ell=\mathrm{MinCut}(G)\). For each positive integer _N_ and each nonempty proper subset \(S\subset V(G)\), Lemmas A.2 and A.3 give

\(\mathsf{Q}(\mathsf{GT}_2(G)^{\otimes_KN})\le\mathrm{FR}_S(\mathsf{GT}_2(G)^{\otimes_KN})=2^{N|\delta_G(S)|}.\)

Taking _N_-th roots, then the limit as \(N\rightarrow\infty\), and minimizing over _S_ proves \(\widetilde{\mathsf{Q}}(\mathsf{GT}_2(G))\le 2^\ell\).

If _G_ is disconnected, then \(\ell=0\). The tensor is nonzero, so its subrank is at least 1, and the upper bound proves the claim. If _G_ is connected and _k_=2, then _G=K_<sub>2</sub> and GT<sub>2</sub>(_G_)=I<sub>2</sub>(2), whose asymptotic subrank is 2. We may therefore assume that _G_ is connected and \(k\ge 3\).

Put _m_=|_E(G_)| and \(d=m-\ell\). Fix integral vectors \((c_e)_{e\in E(G)}\) as in Lemma B.2, and write _c<sub>e</sub>_=(_c_<sub>_e,_1</sub>_,...,c<sub>e,d</sub>_) for every \(e\in E(G)\). For every vertex _v_, let _E<sub>v</sub>_ be the set of edges incident to<tbc>

_v_. Because \(\mathrm{deg}(v)\ge\ell\), the family \((c_e)_{e\in E(G)\backslash E_v}\) has at most \(m-\ell=d\) members and is linearly independent. We first select a large set of edge labelings. Hence distinct labelings in F_g_ give distinct basis vectors at every

vertex. Enumerate the _R_ labelings and, on each leg, map the basis vector belonging to the _h_-th labeling to \(e_h^{(R)}\) for \(0\le h\le R-1\), while sending unused coordinates to zero.
